This study provides a rigorous a priori error analysis for two-layer neural networks used to compute high-dimensional Schrödinger eigenfunctions. We demonstrate that the approximation error diminishes at an algebraic rate as the network size increases, a finding that holds regardless of the input dimension. Furthermore, we establish that the required sample complexity for data-driven methods remains independent of the dimension, thereby addressing the issue of the curse of dimensionality. These theoretical results are validated through numerical experiments. The paper's primary contributions are as follows: (i) We derive an explicit upper bound for the generalization error of two-layer neural networks when utilizing data generated by a neural network-based Galerkin method; (ii) We prove that this error bound remains independent of the dimension, effectively resolving the curse of dimensionality; (iii) We present explicit error estimates for both the neural network approximation and the neural Galerkin approximation. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to verify the accuracy of our theoretical findings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Neural-Network-for-Schrodinger-Eigenvalue-Problem. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a prominent category of machine learning models designed to process sequential data. This study examines their efficacy in modeling the neuronal activity of the nematode *C. elegans*. We demonstrate that RNNs can be trained to replicate the activity of individual neurons and specific neural circuits, achieving performance that matches or surpasses that of linear regression models. Furthermore, we explore the application of time series regression using Lasso and Ridge regression to uncover the connectivity patterns of neural circuits. Our findings indicate that these methods can identify connectivity patterns consistent with established biological knowledge. Finally, we illustrate how Lasso regression can forecast the activity of neurons within uncharacterized circuits. Collectively, these results suggest that time series regression offers a valuable complementary approach to RNNs for modeling neuronal behavior. This paper aims to identify all maximal subgroups $H$ of the group $G = \mathrm{SL}(2,p)$, where $p$ is a prime, such that the pair $(G,H)$ constitutes a strong Gelfand pair. Our findings indicate that, aside from the cases where $H$ is the normalizer of a Sylow 2-subgroup or a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$, the pair $(G,H)$ is a strong Gelfand pair if and only if $H$ is the normalizer of a Singer subgroup. This result extends the work of P. Terwilliger, who previously established that for any prime $p$, the pair $(\mathrm{SL}(2,p), B)$ forms a strong Gelfand pair, where $B$ represents a Borel subgroup of $G$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the pair $(\mathrm{SL}(2,2^k), B)$ is also a strong Gelfand pair for all positive integers $k$. Finally, we examine the specific instances where $G = \mathrm{SL}(2,11)$ and $G = \mathrm{SL}(2,19)$. In these cases, we determine that the pair $(G,H)$ is a strong Gelfand pair if and only if $H$ is either a Borel subgroup or the normalizer of a Singer subgroup. These results are significant as they provide a complete classification of strong Gelfand pairs for $\mathrm{SL}(2,11)$ and $\mathrm{SL}(2,19)$. Furthermore, we note that the pair $(G,H)$ is a strong Gelfand pair if and only if $H$ is a Borel subgroup or a normalizer of a Singer subgroup, provided that $p$ is a prime satisfying $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Consequently, we have successfully classified all strong Gelfand pairs for $\mathrm{SL}(2,p)$ under the condition $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. This work also generalizes the results of P. Terwilliger. This study investigates the electric and magnetic dipole moments of the recently observed $P_{cs}(4459)$ and $P_{\Xi c}(4448)$ states, which are candidates for hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks containing a single strange quark. By employing a relativistic three-body framework, we calculate these moments and compare our findings with existing experimental data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the electromagnetic form factors of the $P_{cs}(4459)$ and $P_{\Xi c}(4448)$ states exhibit distinct behaviors across different momentum transfers. Finally, we discuss the potential for future experimental measurements to further explore the internal structure of these exotic hadrons. This paper establishes that all finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras are nilpotent. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for their nilpotency index, which is determined by the algebra's dimension. Additionally, we provide an explicit construction of a non-nilpotent Zinbiel algebra over any field with characteristic greater than 2. The study also examines the relationship between Zinbiel algebras and Novikov algebras, proving that any Zinbiel algebra where the associated Novikov algebra is nilpotent must itself be nilpotent. Finally, the nilpotency of Zinbiel algebras is demonstrated through the lens of representation theory. These findings are derived from the author's thesis, which was supervised by Professor Wei Sheng Liu. The work includes a detailed analysis of the classification of low-dimensional Zinbiel algebras. This paper investigates the scattering theory for the cubic inhomogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring an inverse square potential in three dimensions. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Cauchy problem remains globally well-posed within the energy space $H^1(\mathbb{R}^3)\times H^1(\mathbb{R}^3)$, with scattering established for initial data possessing sufficiently small $H^1$-norms. Furthermore, we prove that the scattering operator is continuous within this same space. These findings extend previous results by the authors, which were limited to the one-dimensional case. The primary instrument employed is a novel Morawetz-type estimate. Additionally, we examine the critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation and demonstrate that global well-posedness and scattering hold for small initial data in the critical Sobolev space $H^{s_c}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. Finally, we establish the continuous dependence of the scattering operator on this critical space. The methodology utilized here is applicable to a broader class of inhomogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations. Notably, our results represent the first global well-posedness and scattering theory for the cubic inhomogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equation in three dimensions. This work also advances the theory for the critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation with an inverse square potential. We introduce a novel class of migration processes termed "migration-contagion processes," which function as discrete-time mechanisms for spreading infectious diseases. In this framework, infected individuals migrate to new locations, where they transmit the disease to healthy individuals upon arrival. We establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing that the proportion of infected individuals converges to a stationary distribution. Furthermore, we derive conditions ensuring the existence of a unique stationary distribution and demonstrate its ergodicity. Finally, we present a specific example of such a process and analyze its properties. This instance represents a discrete-time adaptation of a continuous-time migration-diffusion process previously examined by the author. Additionally, we explore the relationship between migration-diffusion and migration-contagion processes. The findings are applicable to both human and animal populations. The analysis relies on the theory of stochastic processes, specifically branching processes and Markov chains. This work functions as a discrete-time counterpart to the author's earlier study on migration-diffusion processes. We confirm the existence of a resonant chain in the K2-183 system, where three planets orbit in a 3:2:1 sequence. This discovery was achieved by analyzing the transit timing variations of the innermost planet, K2-183b, using the Generalized Least Squares method. Our findings indicate that the system's resonant chain is more stable than previously thought, with the 3:2 resonant pair being particularly robust. Additionally, we determined the system's age to be 1.1 billion years and estimated the planets' densities to be 1.8, 1.2, and 1.1 g/cm³, respectively. These results suggest that the planets are primarily composed of silicate and iron. Finally, we calculated the planets' equilibrium temperatures to be 300, 200, and 170 K. These characteristics imply that the planets are likely to possess atmospheres, making them promising candidates for future atmospheric studies. Furthermore, the planets' sizes and temperatures position them as potential members of the "habitable zone." Consequently, K2-183 represents a valuable target for further investigation into the formation and evolution of planetary systems. This study underscores the significance of transit timing variations in elucidating the dynamics of exoplanetary systems. Amorphous ice exhibits two primary structural forms: low-density (LDA) and high-density (HDA). Recent findings indicate that HDA ice contains a minor fraction of crystalline ice domains, a phenomenon termed "crystal-ice." This study investigates the potential existence of crystal-ice domains within LDA ice. Utilizing a machine learning approach, we constructed a dataset of ice structures derived from molecular dynamics simulations of water confined in silica pores. Our results demonstrate that LDA ice possesses a higher propensity for crystal-ice formation compared to HDA ice. Furthermore, we identified a specific local structural motif that facilitates this formation in LDA ice, which is less prevalent in HDA ice. These insights offer a deeper understanding of the structural characteristics of amorphous ice and the mechanisms driving its crystallization. Additionally, the methodology employed is applicable to other amorphous materials. This study presents high-resolution Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM) images of graphite, gold, and silicon surfaces, accompanied by a detailed analysis of their respective Local Density of States (LDOS). By employing constant current and constant height scanning modes, we achieved atomic-level imaging of these materials. The experimental data were compared against theoretical models to interpret the observed STM features. Furthermore, we utilized STM to measure the height of individual atomic steps on the surfaces of gold and graphite. These findings offer valuable insights into the electronic structures of the examined materials and demonstrate the exceptional capability of STM for nanoscale imaging. The research underscores the significance of STM in advancing nanotechnology and materials science. Additionally, the paper includes a comprehensive tutorial on STM, detailing its operating principles, advantages, and applications. This educational content is intended to assist students and researchers in gaining a foundational understanding of the technique. The study concludes by outlining potential future directions for STM research. Overall, this work serves as a thorough examination of STM imaging and measurements, providing a valuable resource for those interested in the field. By examining the Isabelle AFP, we identify that 10% of its theorems are duplicates, 15% are subsumed by others, and 20% are superseded. Our findings indicate that this method is both scalable and effective. Finally, we explore the potential of this technique for improving other large-scale formal libraries. Ultra-low-frequency (ULF) waves within the Earth's magnetosphere are typically visualized through spectrograms, which plot signal intensity against time and frequency. However, these waves can also be perceived as sound, with their acoustic representation determined by the chosen mapping of ULF data to audible frequencies. This study evaluates various mapping techniques and their resulting auditory characteristics. We demonstrate that the most effective approach involves mapping ULF data to audible frequencies in a way that preserves the relative durations of events. Furthermore, we illustrate how this method enables the creation of a magnetosphere "soundscape" that remains consistent across different ULF frequency bands. This soundscape offers a novel perspective on magnetospheric dynamics, revealing temporal variations in ULF wave power that are often obscured in spectrograms. Additionally, we provide a Python-based tool to facilitate the generation of these audible representations. By making ULF data accessible to a broader scientific community, we aim to inspire new research directions and innovative approaches to understanding the magnetosphere. This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of a four-dimensional charged, rotating dilaton black brane within logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics. The analysis covers both the nonrotating limit and the general rotating case. We determine the horizon radius, temperature, entropy, and Gibbs free energy for both scenarios. Furthermore, we explore the phase structure of the system, specifically focusing on the Hawking-Page phase transition. Finally, we investigate the stability of the black brane using the canonical ensemble. These findings are compared with those of other theories, and the results are discussed in detail. Additionally, we calculate the horizon radius for the corresponding anti-de Sitter space. Finally, we present the thermodynamic phase diagrams for both the nonrotating and rotating cases. This work extends our previous research on four-dimensional charged dilaton black branes in logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics, where we analyzed the thermodynamics of nonrotating configurations. Our earlier study demonstrated that the phase structure of nonrotating charged dilaton black branes in logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics differs from that in Maxwell electrodynamics. In this paper, we further investigate the thermodynamics of the rotating case. We show that the phase structure of charged, rotating dilaton black branes in logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics also differs from that in Maxwell electrodynamics. These findings suggest that the phase structure of black holes is sensitive to the choice of electromagnetic field. This research contributes to the broader effort of understanding the thermodynamics of black holes and black branes. Additionally, it offers insights into the phase structure of black holes, which is crucial for advancing our understanding of the universe. Finally, this work may contribute to the development of new theories of gravity. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the model; Section 3 derives the thermodynamic quantities; Section 4 analyzes the phase structure; and Section 5 concludes the study. The $q$-deformation of the Cuntz algebra, denoted as $\mathcal{O}_q$, is defined by a parameter $q$ within the closed unit disk. This paper presents a continuous deformation of the Fock representation of $\mathcal{O}_q$ that links the Fock representations of the CCR and CAR algebras. Consequently, the representations of $\mathcal{O}_q$ associated with CCR and CAR are connected through a continuous family of representations of $\mathcal{O}_q$. This construction relies on a specific representation of $\mathcal{O}_q$ that acts as a "twist" between the two algebras. Furthermore, this methodology yields a novel representation of the CCR algebra. The study also examines the irreducibility of these representations and their connection to the $q$-deformation of the symplectic group. Finally, the paper explores the implications of this construction for the quantum plane. The research was conducted within the framework of the "Quantum Groups and their Applications" project, which is funded by the Ministry of Education and Science of the Russian Federation under grant No. 14.B25.31.0001. The photoevaporation model, which posits that stellar ultraviolet radiation carves out a gap in the outer disk, has long been the primary explanation for the observed radio emission from the TW Hydrae association. However, recent findings suggest that magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk winds might also account for these radio signals. This study aims to differentiate between these two models by analyzing the spectral index and spatial distribution of the radio emission. We utilized the 2018 and 2019 observations of the TW Hydrae association from the VLA to measure the spectral index and determine the emission's spatial extent. Our results indicate that the emission is confined within 100 au of the star, a finding that contradicts the predictions of the photoevaporation model. Furthermore, we calculated the total flux density of the radio emission to be $1.1 \pm 0.1$ mJy, with a spectral index of $0.5 \pm 0.1$. These measurements align with the characteristics of MHD disk wind models. Consequently, our findings support the hypothesis that MHD disk winds are the dominant source of radio emission in the TW Hydrae association. This conclusion is reinforced by the spectral index, which is consistent with optically thick MHD disk wind models. Additionally, we estimated the mass accretion rate to be $\dot{M} \sim 10^{-9} M_{\odot} \text{ yr}^{-1}$, a value consistent with the observed radio emission. Finally, we determined the magnetic field strength to be $B \sim 10$ G, a figure that is consistent with the observed radio emission and the estimated mass accretion rate. These results collectively suggest that MHD disk winds are the primary source of radio emission in the TW Hydrae association. A function mapping natural numbers to natural numbers is considered near exponential if it is sandwiched between two near exponential functions. This paper demonstrates the existence of infinite finitely generated groups whose residual finiteness growth is near exponential. Furthermore, for any given near exponential growth rate, we construct a family of groups exhibiting that specific growth. Additionally, we establish a group that is both residually finite and locally finite, while also being near exponential. Finally, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for a finitely generated group to possess near exponential residual finiteness growth. This condition requires the group to be residually finite, locally finite, and near exponential. The methodology for proving this result draws inspiration from the work of Olshanskii and Sapir. The paper concludes with several open questions. The authors gratefully acknowledge the insightful discussions they had with Sapir. This study examines the stability of a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam connected to two elastic springs via a star-shaped graph. The system's dynamics are governed by a conservative group that maps initial data in the energy space to future states. We establish the orbital stability of the standing wave solution within the energy space. Furthermore, we demonstrate local stability for this standing wave in the energy space, with the stability radius quantified by the distance to the nearest bifurcation point. Finally, we prove global stability for small initial data in the energy space. These findings extend previous results by removing the requirement for the graph to be a tree. Additionally, we provide a complete spectral analysis of the associated linear operator. The methodology employed relies on a novel approach to analyzing the spectrum of the linear operator, which may have broader applications in related fields. The paper concludes with an illustrative example. This work is part of a series; the preceding study can be found at arXiv:2009.00009. The subsequent study will be available at arXiv:2009.00008. We introduce a machine learning approach to estimate nuclear masses, utilizing a training set derived from the finite-range droplet model (FRDM) and augmented with experimental data. This method achieves a root-mean-square deviation of 0.65 MeV for nuclei with $Z \leq 82$, a figure comparable to the FRDM's deviation from experimental masses. For neutron-rich nuclei beyond the FRDM domain, the model predicts masses with an accuracy of 1 MeV, a precision sufficient for $r$-process investigations. The study also examines the model's performance regarding nuclear binding energies, separation energies, and two-neutron separation energies. Furthermore, we apply the machine learning framework to predict the masses of superheavy nuclei. Finally, we explore the potential of this technique to identify new magic numbers. These findings demonstrate that machine learning serves as a powerful tool for investigating nuclear masses. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robertkoster/MLnucmass. Sapphire is extensively utilized in quantum technologies due to its exceptional dielectric properties. However, the intrinsic dielectric loss tangent of high-purity sapphire remains poorly understood, as it is obscured by surface losses and the microwave cavity's geometry factor. This study presents a precision measurement of the microwave dielectric loss tangent for high-purity sapphire, achieving a sensitivity of 1 part per billion. The results indicate that the dielectric loss tangent of high-purity sapphire is approximately $1.5 \times 10^{-9}$ at 5 GHz, with a temperature dependence of $10^{-11}$ per Kelvin. These findings establish a baseline for the dielectric loss of high-purity sapphire, which is essential for the development of high-performance superconducting quantum devices. Furthermore, the measurement technique is applicable to other dielectric materials. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/quantum-dielectric-loss/sapphire-loss-measurement. This study addresses two-stage robust optimization problems where the first-stage decision is a vector and the second-stage involves binary variables. The analysis assumes that the uncertainty set consists of all binary vectors with a fixed number of ones, a scenario applicable to various practical contexts. We demonstrate that the Lagrangian dual of the resulting min-max problem can be formulated as a mixed-integer program. Furthermore, we establish that this dual problem is solvable in polynomial time when the second-stage objective function is linear, and we provide a method to derive an optimal solution for the original problem from the dual's solution. Additionally, we extend these findings to cases where the second-stage problem is a mixed-integer program. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed approach. The paper concludes with a discussion on the implications of these results.

Keywords: Robust Optimization, Two-Stage Optimization, Binary Uncertainties, Lagrangian Dual, Mixed-Integer Programming.

This paper introduces H4M, a heterogeneous, multi-source, multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-distributional dataset designed for socioeconomic analytics within Beijing. The dataset comprises four distinct data sources: (1) Beijing Taxi GPS trajectories, (2) Beijing Taxi GPS data enriched with social media information, (3) Beijing Taxi GPS data augmented with weather conditions, and (4) Beijing Taxi GPS data combined with both weather and social media. Furthermore, the study addresses the challenges associated with data collection and processing, and outlines the dataset's potential applications. Pattern mining has become a fundamental technique for extracting valuable insights from vast datasets. However, the sheer volume of discovered patterns often overwhelms users, making it difficult to identify the most relevant ones. This paper introduces a visual approach that enables users to explore and select patterns based on their specific needs. By leveraging the visual representation of patterns, this method facilitates a more intuitive and user-centric exploration process. Our approach is conceptually straightforward, relying on a straightforward reduction from the well-known Clique problem. This finding implies that the streaming algorithms developed by Fischer et al. [STOC 2020] are optimal. Additionally, Fischer et al. [STOC 2020] conjectured that their algorithm could be enhanced to achieve an $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ upper bound; we confirm this conjecture. We present a comprehensive investigation into the non-analytic momentum dependence of the spin susceptibility in the paramagnetic phase of three-dimensional Heisenberg magnets. This behavior is derived from the non-analytic component of the momentum-dependent self-energy, which originates from spin fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that this non-analytic contribution significantly influences the momentum-space structure of the spin susceptibility. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the non-linear spin fluctuation theory, incorporating this non-analytic dependence, yields distinct values for critical exponents compared to the self-consistent renormalization (SCRT) theory, which relies on a decoupling approximation. Specifically, the critical exponents for the correlation length ($\nu$), specific heat ($\alpha$), and the correlation function at the critical point ($\eta$) are determined as $\nu=0.67$, $\alpha=0.08$, and $\eta=0.06$, respectively. These results align closely with the most precise numerical estimates available. Additionally, we calculate the critical exponent $\gamma$ as $1.22$ and the ratio $R_C$ as $0.31$, both of which are in good agreement with the best numerical estimates. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the critical behavior of the 3D Heisenberg model. This study investigates the linear and nonlinear Hall conductivities of interacting disordered systems, specifically focusing on the half-filled Landau level in graphene. By employing the functional renormalization group method, we analyze how interactions and disorder influence these nonlinear Hall responses. Our findings indicate that while the nonlinear Hall conductivity remains robust against interaction effects, it is significantly suppressed by disorder. In contrast, the linear Hall conductivity is unaffected by interactions but is strongly suppressed by disorder, a result that aligns with the established quantum Hall effect. Furthermore, we observe that the nonlinear Hall conductivity exhibits a distinct peak at the Dirac point, a feature that diminishes as interaction strength increases. Finally, we demonstrate that the nonlinear Hall conductivity can be tuned by adjusting the interaction strength, offering a viable pathway for experimental observation. These results hold significant implications for the development of novel electronic devices. Additionally, our methodology is applicable to other interacting disordered systems, including those with inversion symmetry breaking. This paper serves as a tutorial on applying direct transcription methods to solve dynamic optimization problems, using a ventilator control case study to demonstrate the approach. The objective is to minimize the time required for a dual-patient ventilator to reach a target state, defined by specific lung volume and flow rates, for two patients with varying respiratory conditions. The study evaluates two nonlinear programming solvers—IPOPT and KNITRO—against two direct transcription schemes: the pseudospectral collocation method and the direct shooting method. Results indicate that the pseudospectral collocation scheme outperforms the direct shooting method, and that both IPOPT and KNITRO are effective for this application. Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed comparison of the computational complexities associated with these methods. Finally, the authors conclude by outlining potential future research directions. The source code for the simulations is accessible at https://github.com/AniruddhaKumar1999/Ventilator-Control. The corresponding MATLAB files can be found at https://github.com/AniruddhaKumar1999/Ventilator-Control/tree/master/MATLAB%20files. The MATLAB files are also available in the supplementary material. Additionally, the authors' GitHub repository includes a video walkthrough of the paper. This tutorial is intended to assist researchers in selecting the most appropriate direct transcription scheme and solver for their specific dynamic optimization problems. This study examines the electronic characteristics of monolayer and few-layer MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, WS$_2$, and WSe$_2$ using density functional theory (DFT) and $G$W calculations. We analyze how these properties vary with layer count, specifically focusing on the work function, ionization energy, and electron affinity. Our findings indicate that the work function decreases as the number of layers increases, whereas both ionization energy and electron affinity rise with additional layers. Furthermore, we observe that the work function is lower in Mo-based compounds compared to W-based ones, and MoS$_2$ exhibits the smallest work function among the group. These results offer valuable insights for tailoring the electronic properties of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) for specific applications. Additionally, we compare our computed band structures with experimental data to validate the accuracy of our computational approach. Finally, we explore the potential of these materials as photocatalysts for hydrogen production. The source code used for all calculations is accessible at https://github.com/abhisheksingh1997/TMD. Delta lenses provide a formal framework for modeling bidirectional model transformations. This paper introduces a novel approach to model-driven learning, which leverages this framework to propagate data-driven model changes. We demonstrate that various supervised learning techniques can be viewed as change propagation within delta lenses, with the specific method emerging from the lens's properties. Furthermore, we illustrate how this learning-as-change-propagation concept can be applied to construct a model-driven learning framework for generating machine learning models. This framework utilizes model-to-model transformations to derive training data and to propagate both data-driven and model-driven modifications. Finally, we validate the framework's effectiveness through an experimental evaluation. (2021). The primary distinction lies in the inclusion of a more comprehensive experimental evaluation, which examines the framework's effectiveness across a broader range of learning tasks. Additionally, the current version offers a more detailed exposition of the approach, including a more rigorous definition of delta lenses and a more thorough analysis of the relationship between change propagation and supervised learning. The paper also features a more extensive discussion of the approach's limitations and future research directions. The experimental evaluation has been expanded to cover a wider variety of learning tasks. Finally, the related work section has been significantly expanded to incorporate more recent studies. This study investigates the steady-state solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations governing rarefied gas flows. We introduce a novel iterative approach utilizing a time-dependent formulation, which integrates a newly developed implicit scheme for the Navier-Stokes equations with a standard implicit method for the Boltzmann equation. The efficacy of this method is evaluated across three test cases: flow around a sphere, a shock tube, and a lid-driven cavity. Results indicate that steady-state solutions can be achieved within dozens of iterations, demonstrating the method's robustness and high efficiency. Furthermore, the implicit scheme successfully eliminates the stringent time-step constraints typically imposed by explicit methods. Finally, the approach is validated against existing analytical and numerical benchmarks. These findings confirm that the proposed method is both accurate and efficient for solving steady rarefied gas flows. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/NavierStokes. The Horizon-10T experiment, situated at the Pierre Auger Observatory, is designed to investigate ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and high-energy gamma rays. Its unique capability to measure the Cherenkov light polarization vector in the ground plane enables the determination of the polarization ellipse's orientation angle, a metric that has proven valuable for analyzing UHECR composition and anisotropy. This study examines the characteristics of a distinct cluster of events identified in the data, which exhibits a significantly different polarization orientation angle distribution compared to the rest of the sample. We explore the hypothesis that this cluster originates from a specific source and investigate whether axion quark nuggets (AQN) could serve as such a source. Our analysis indicates that AQNs are unlikely to be the source of this cluster. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the observed cluster is consistent with a source of UHECRs possessing a proton fraction of approximately 10%. Finally, we outline the potential of the experiment to detect UHECR sources and discuss the prospects for future research. We demonstrate that for any Siegel modular form of degree $n$ with Fourier coefficients divisible by a prime $p$ at least to the power $p^{n-1}$, the form must be identically zero. This finding extends the work of Yoshida, who established a similar result for forms of weight at least $p^{n-2}$. Furthermore, we provide an explicit example of a Siegel modular form of degree 3, weight 1, and level 1 whose coefficients are all divisible by 13. Our proof relies on the theory of Gross-Zagier Siegel modular forms, drawing inspiration from the methodology used by the second author in a previous publication. Additionally, we present a generalization of Yoshida's result to the context of Siegel modular forms with half-integral weights. Finally, we explore the relationship between our findings and the divisibility of the Fourier coefficients of the Siegel-Eisenstein series of degree 2 and weight 2 by the prime 11. This latter aspect is motivated by the recent work of Bertolini, Darmon, and Gillard, which connects the $p$-adic valuation of the Fourier coefficients of this specific Siegel-Eisenstein series to the divisibility of the prime $p$ by 3. Our results indicate that the Yoshida-Yamagata divisibility pattern holds for $p=13$. However, we also identify a discrepancy between our findings and those of Bertolini, Darmon, and Gillard, suggesting that their result may require refinement. This potential refinement could have significant implications for the study of the Gross-Zagier-Darmon conjecture. The paper concludes with a discussion of several open questions. The Pauli exclusion principle governs the behavior of fermions, such as electrons, by preventing them from occupying the same quantum state. In two dimensions, this principle manifests in the fractional quantum Hall effect, where electron interactions generate exotic quasiparticles with fractional charges and statistics. This study examines a classical model of charged particles on a 2D plane subject to strong repulsive forces, which unexpectedly yields quantum-like structures known as "Pauli crystals." These formations exhibit remarkable stability and can be analyzed using statistical mechanics. Our findings indicate that Pauli crystals represent the most probable configurations within the grand canonical ensemble, thereby offering a classical framework for understanding the quantum Hall effect. Furthermore, we explore the broader implications of this model for both quantum and classical physics. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkennedy/pauli-crystals. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN), a computational framework designed to address time-varying matrix problems. ZNN is defined by its state equation, which drives the state vector toward zero at an exponential rate. The approach is particularly effective for time-varying matrix problems, which are prevalent in control systems, image processing, and machine learning. The study begins by outlining the design principles of ZNN and introducing the Zeroing Neural Dynamic (ZND) model. Subsequently, it reviews the application of ZNN to solving time-varying linear equations, time-varying matrix inversion, and time-varying pseudo-inversion. Furthermore, the paper examines the extension of ZNN to time-varying matrix factorization, including singular value decomposition (SVD) and QR factorization. Finally, the authors propose a novel SVD algorithm based on ZNN, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods through numerical simulations. The paper concludes with a discussion on future research directions. This work serves as a foundational resource for researchers interested in applying neural networks to time-varying matrix problems. Wide-field x-ray optics are essential for numerous applications, including x-ray astronomy, microscopy, and lithography. This study introduces a new optimization framework designed to determine optimal prescriptions for these wide-field x-ray optical systems. The process begins by defining a target optical prescription, characterized by its field of view, magnification, and source-to-image distance. Subsequently, a set of candidate optical elements is selected, and their parameters are optimized to replicate the target prescription as closely as possible. The framework employs a least-squares error function to quantify the discrepancy between the desired and actual optical behavior, utilizing ray-tracing simulations to evaluate this error. To address the high dimensionality of the optimization problem, the method incorporates a genetic algorithm. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through the optimization of a Cassegrain telescope and a Wolter III telescope. Furthermore, the framework is applied to optimize a multi-mirror system, where individual mirrors are arranged to cover distinct regions of the target field of view. This strategy successfully reduces the root mean square error of the optical system by up to 50% compared to a single-mirror configuration. Ultimately, this work establishes a robust foundation for the design of wide-field x-ray optical systems. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1999/WideFieldOptics. The Bloch theorem is fundamental to solid-state physics, yet its validity within magnetic fields remains a subject of debate. This study examines a system of graphene layers twisted by a specific angle, subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field. We demonstrate that the Bloch theorem is restored when the magnetic flux through the moiré unit cell reaches $2\pi$ flux quanta. Under these conditions, the system exhibits a reentrant insulating state at half-filling, characterized by a flat band with four-fold degeneracy. This reemergence of insulating behavior is attributed to the restoration of the chiral symmetry inherent in the moiré lattice. Furthermore, we explore the potential for lifting this flat band by introducing a sublattice-dependent potential. These findings offer a pathway to investigate the quantum Hall effect in graphene and may inspire the design of novel quantum materials. Additionally, our results provide a theoretical basis for recent experimental observations of a reentrant insulating state in twisted bilayer graphene. Finally, we extend the $2\pi$ flux theorem to general two-dimensional systems. Our analysis reveals that the $2\pi$ flux theorem is equivalent to the commensurability between the magnetic flux and the area of the Brillouin zone, a condition that can be achieved by adjusting the magnetic field strength. Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge in power system operations, involving the determination of optimal generation schedules for thermal generators to meet demand at the lowest cost while adhering to various operational constraints. Although mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is the standard method for solving UC, its computational demands often render it impractical for real-time applications. Consequently, numerous heuristic and approximate methods have been developed to accelerate UC solutions. This paper introduces a machine learning-based approach to enhance the efficiency of UC solvers. Specifically, the proposed method utilizes a neural network to forecast generator costs, thereby enabling the rapid screening of constraints. The study evaluates the method's performance using the IEEE 118-bus system. Results demonstrate that the approach significantly reduces computation time while maintaining high solution quality. Furthermore, the method proves robust against variations in load levels and generation costs. Finally, the paper provides an in-depth analysis of the model's architecture and training strategy. The Kitaev material $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ exhibits a complex magnetic ground state, with the interplay between Kitaev interactions and spin-orbit-coupling-induced Heisenberg exchange driving a quantum phase transition to a Kitaev spin liquid. This study employs high-pressure magnetization and neutron scattering to investigate the evolution of magnetic order in this compound. Our findings reveal that increasing pressure suppresses antiferromagnetic order, leading to a collapse of the Néel temperature at approximately 10 GPa. Concurrently, a pressure-induced dimerization of the Li$_2$IrO$_3$ lattice is observed, which we attribute to the suppression of antiferromagnetic order. These results offer new insights into the competition between Kitaev and Heisenberg interactions in this system. Furthermore, the observed dimerization suggests that the Kitaev spin liquid phase may be stabilized at pressures exceeding 10 GPa. This work underscores the critical role of lattice distortions in the phase diagram of Kitaev materials. Additionally, the results provide a foundation for future research aimed at realizing the elusive Kitaev spin liquid phase in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$. Finally, the pressure-induced dimerization observed in this study may have broader implications for other Kitaev materials, offering a potential pathway for engineering Kitaev spin liquid phases. Synthetic control methods have gained significant traction for causal inference, particularly when randomized experiments are absent. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework to elucidate the mechanisms behind synthetic controls. Our approach integrates two key components: a novel identification strategy for the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) and a new inference methodology. Identification is achieved by leveraging the causal structure of the data alongside the assumption that the control unit is proximal to the treated unit. Proximity is defined as the existence of a linear combination of the control's pre-treatment covariates that closely approximates the post-treatment trajectory of the treated unit. We demonstrate that this linear combination serves as a valid proxy for the counterfactual outcome had the treated unit not received the intervention. Furthermore, we propose a novel inference method that utilizes the identified linear combination to construct a counterfactual outcome series. This framework accommodates scenarios where the treated unit is a single entity or a collection of multiple units. Empirical applications are provided to illustrate the framework's utility. The results indicate that synthetic controls yield reliable inference, with the proposed method outperforming existing alternatives in terms of statistical power. Additionally, the framework offers a unified explanation for the success of synthetic control techniques. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/SyntheticControl. We introduce a novel method for generating and accelerating electrons within a plasma wakefield, utilizing a laser pulse that self-steepens due to the plasma's Kerr nonlinearity. This self-steepening effect creates a sharp intensity gradient at the pulse's trailing edge, which injects electrons into the wakefield. The injected electrons are then accelerated to high energies by the resulting plasma wakefield. This mechanism is applicable to both linear and circularly polarized laser pulses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the polarization state of the laser pulse can be manipulated to control the injection of electrons into the plasma wakefield. These findings offer a new approach for generating and accelerating high-energy electrons using a single laser pulse. Additionally, this technique could facilitate the development of compact, high-energy, high-peak-current, and high-brightness electron sources. We have also conducted a numerical simulation of an electron bunch injector based on this proposed mechanism. The simulation results indicate that the proposed method can achieve electron injection with a low energy spread of approximately 1.5% and a high peak current of about 1.5 kA. These outcomes suggest that the proposed mechanism is viable for practical implementation. Finally, we have conducted a series of numerical simulations to investigate the influence of various parameters on electron injection and acceleration. These simulations reveal that the polarization state of the laser pulse significantly impacts the injection process. Specifically, linear polarization yields the highest electron density and current, whereas circular polarization produces the highest electron energy. These findings provide valuable insights for optimizing the proposed mechanism for electron injection and acceleration. This study examines the generalized three-dimensional Ermakov system, extending the classical model by incorporating an additional term in its equations of motion. The analysis focuses on determining the conditions under which this system exhibits symmetries and conserves quantities. Furthermore, the paper establishes the relationship between the system's linearizable properties and its conservation laws. Finally, the findings are extended to the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. Additionally, the classical three-dimensional case is revisited to demonstrate the application of these results. A key finding is that the generalized system can be linearized via a point transformation, whereas the classical system requires linearization through a gauge transformation. Finally, the paper explores the link between conservation laws and the linearization of the generalized Ermakov system. These findings are applicable to various physical contexts, including the study of charged particles within electromagnetic fields. The research concludes with several illustrative examples. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the generalized three-dimensional Ermakov system and outlines the linearization method; Section 3 investigates the existence of conservation laws; Section 4 addresses the linearization of the system; Section 5 extends the analysis to the generalized $n$-dimensional case; and Section 6 applies these findings to the classical charged particle problem. The paper concludes with a discussion of the results. Additionally, an appendix provides a detailed derivation of the linearization method. Keywords: Generalized three-dimensional Ermakov system; Linearization; Conservation laws. A directed graph is semi-transitive if it lacks any semi-transitive cycles of length greater than two, where a cycle $(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k,v_1)$ is semi-transitive when the edges $(v_1,v_2), (v_2,v_3), \ldots, (v_k,v_1)$ form a transitive tournament. A graph is orientable if it possesses a semi-transitive orientation. This paper demonstrates that every split graph is orientable and provides an algorithm to determine a semi-transitive orientation for any given split graph. Furthermore, we establish that for every split graph $G$, the number of distinct semi-transitive orientations is bounded by $2^{O(n^2)}$, where $n$ represents the count of vertices in $G$. Additionally, we prove that the orientability of split graphs cannot be characterized by any finite set of obstructions. Finally, we present an algorithm to compute a semi-transitive orientation for any split graph in $O(mn)$ time, where $m$ denotes the number of edges. This approach improves upon the previously best-known algorithm, which operated in $O(mn^2)$ time. The authors' earlier work on this topic can be found in [1].

The identification of tau leptons is a critical component of physics analyses at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The upcoming Rubin Observatory's Vera C. Rubin Telescope is expected to generate petabytes of data annually, a volume that will necessitate the use of machine learning for classification tasks. This study examines the application of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) for this purpose, specifically evaluating their ability to quantify uncertainty in predictions. We demonstrate that BNNs can achieve performance comparable to that of standard neural networks. Furthermore, we show that the uncertainty metrics provided by BNNs offer a distinct advantage over standard networks, particularly when dealing with noisy datasets. Finally, we illustrate that BNNs are capable of identifying the boundaries of their training data, thereby enabling the detection of out-of-distribution samples. These findings suggest that BNNs will be highly valuable for the data analysis tasks anticipated from the Rubin Observatory. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/mauricio-ramos/BNNs-for-Rubin. These findings provide valuable insights for the design of fibers intended for applications involving intermodal Brillouin scattering. The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) involves selecting a subset of items to maximize the union of their associated element sets within a given weight limit. This problem is NP-hard and serves as a generalization of the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP), which is a specific case where each item can cover at most one set. While several heuristics exist for these problems, they often suffer from slow convergence. This paper introduces a novel local search algorithm designed to address both SUKP and BMCP. The method employs a multi-start strategy to generate diverse initial solutions and utilizes a dynamic neighborhood structure to guide the search process. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the study applies these algorithms to real-world data, highlighting their practical applicability. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/LS4SUKP.

This study examines the electromagnetic interaction between an electron or positron and a heavy nucleus during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, provided the particle's transverse momentum remains low. The analysis demonstrates that the electromagnetic field of the nucleus can be modeled as a superposition of two coherent photons. Consequently, the differential cross-section for the electron-nucleus interaction is expressed as the product of two photon fluxes and the cross-section for the corresponding two-photon process. This methodology is applicable to ultra-peripheral collisions involving relativistic heavy ions, where the electromagnetic field of each nucleus is characterized by a broad spectrum of virtual photons. Furthermore, the approach is utilized to calculate the cross-section for electron-positron pair production via two-photon fusion. The results indicate that the proposed formula accurately describes the cross-section across all kinematical regions. These findings are particularly relevant for analyzing experimental data from the LHCb detector at the LHC. This paper introduces a motion planning framework utilizing Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to ensure safety-critical operations for robotic systems within dynamic environments. The proposed method integrates model predictive control (MPC) with a CBF-embedded optimization problem to generate safe trajectories for robots facing uncertain dynamics and environmental conditions. To address the computational demands of solving CBF optimization problems in real-time, the authors propose a computationally efficient approach that transforms the optimization task into a convex form. Furthermore, the study examines the convergence properties of the resulting MPC controller and its associated value function. Finally, the paper validates the proposed methodology through simulation experiments. The results demonstrate that the CBF-MPC approach successfully generates safe trajectories for dynamic robots in uncertain settings, while the convex optimization formulation ensures the necessary real-time performance. Additionally, the simulation outcomes confirm the theoretical findings regarding the MPC controller's convergence properties. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. We examine a family of nonlocal traffic models defined by the conservation law $\partial_t \rho + \partial_x (\rho V(\rho * \rho)) = 0$, where the velocity function is $V(\rho) = \min\{v_{\max}, v_0 \exp(-\rho/v_{\max})\}$ and the kernel is $K(\rho) = v_0 \exp(-\rho/v_0)$. The kernel represents the nonlocal interaction kernel, with $v_{\max}$ and $v_0$ serving as the maximum and initial velocities, respectively. We analyze the singular limit as $v_{\max} \to 0$ and establish the entropy admissibility of this limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entropy solution of the singular limit is attained at a rate of $O(v_{\max})$ in the $L^1$ norm. Finally, we establish the entropy admissibility of the singular limit and prove that this solution is reached at an $O(v_{\max})$ rate within the $L^1$ norm. Additionally, we provide a numerical example to illustrate the theoretical findings. This work extends our previous research in [10], where we derived the same convergence rate for the specific case of $v_0 = v_{\max} = 1$. Our methodology relies on the relative entropy technique, which was originally developed by Dafermos [1] for hyperbolic conservation laws. We also present a novel approach to estimate the entropy production of the nonlocal model, utilizing the properties of the kernel and the relative entropy inequality. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the hyperbolic conservation law framework; Section 3 introduces the nonlocal traffic model; Section 4 presents the main results; Section 5 provides the proofs; and Section 6 offers a numerical example. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper.
Keywords: Nonlocal traffic model, singular limit, entropy admissibility, convergence rate.

Dilation surfaces extend the concept of translation surfaces by allowing local atlases with transition maps that are either translations or anti-translations. This study examines the dynamics of linear flows on dilation surfaces, specifically analyzing the behavior of singular orbits. We demonstrate that for a generic dilation surface, every singular orbit exhibits saddle connection behavior, meaning its trajectory remains confined to a finite union of horizontal cylinders. Furthermore, we establish that the dynamical characteristics of linear flows on dilation surfaces mirror those of translation surfaces, with the primary distinction being that rotation numbers are restricted to 0 or 1/2. Additionally, we prove that the set of dilation surfaces supporting Morse-Smale dynamics is dense within the dilation translation locus. Finally, we provide a characterization of dilation surfaces that admit minimal closed geodesics. These findings are derived through the investigation of the local dynamics of the Teichmüller geodesic flow on the dilation translation locus. As an application, we show that the dilation translation locus contains a dense collection of dilation surfaces where the dilation direction is ergodic. This result contrasts with the situation in translation surfaces, where the set of directions yielding minimal closed geodesics is dense, yet Morse-Smale dilation surfaces exist where such directions do not form a dense set. Consequently, the existence of a dense set of Morse-Smale dilation surfaces does not guarantee the existence of a dense set of directions with minimal closed geodesics. The paper concludes with an outline of the proof for the existence of a dense set of dilation surfaces featuring Morse-Smale dynamics. This proof relies on a novel construction of dilation surfaces with Morse-Smale dynamics, which generalizes the translation surface construction by Avila, Kodysh, and Wu. The core of this construction involves a specific class of dilation surfaces that can be represented as suspension flows of interval exchange transformations. We demonstrate that the translation surfaces within this class constitute a dense subset of the dilation translation locus. This result parallels the recent finding by Avila, Kodysh, and Wu regarding the density of translation surfaces with minimal closed geodesics in the translation translation locus. The proof of this result utilizes the recent classification of dilation surfaces possessing minimal closed geodesics. Finally, we outline the proof of the density of minimal closed geodesics in the dilation translation locus, which follows from the recent work of Avila, Kodysh, and Wu. This study introduces a novel Total Correlation (TC) metric designed to assess functional connectivity within the human brain. TC serves as a multivariate generalization of mutual information, capable of capturing both pairwise and higher-order-order interactions among brain regions. We developed a new algorithm to calculate TC in brain networks, demonstrating its superior accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing multivariate methods. Furthermore, we applied TC to analyze resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project, revealing that it effectively identifies both pairwise and higher-order functional connections. Finally, we utilized TC to investigate the functional connectivity patterns associated with schizophrenia. These findings underscore the potential of TC as a robust metric for characterizing complex brain network dynamics. This paper establishes unitary isomorphisms linking the Clifford algebra-valued Fock space $\mathscr{F}_{\mathbb{G}}$ and the polynomial space $\mathscr{P}_{\mathbb{G}}$ through the Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transform $\mathscr{S}_{\mathbb{G}}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this transform $\mathscr{S}_{\mathbb{G}}$ is unitarily equivalent to the Taylor isomorphism $\mathscr{T}_{\mathbb{G}}$. As a consequence, we derive the reproducing kernel for $\mathscr{F}_{\mathbb{G}}$. Finally, we illustrate the application of these findings by constructing an orthonormal basis for $\mathscr{F}_{\mathbb{G}}$. These results are instrumental in advancing the theory of Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transforms and their applications. Additionally, the methodology employed herein can be extended to other algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transforms. This paper introduces a pathwise conditioning framework for Gaussian processes. Unlike traditional conditioning methods that operate on random vectors, our approach treats the Gaussian process realization as a random function. We derive the conditional distribution of the Gaussian process given observations at specific points along the path. This pathwise conditioning technique enables the construction of a conditional Gaussian process that adheres to a specified pathwise constraint. Furthermore, we apply this pathwise conditioning method to develop a new algorithm for the GPsNN, a neural network architecture designed to model Gaussian processes. The proposed algorithm allows the GPsNN to be conditioned on a specific path, thereby enhancing its predictive accuracy. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the pathwise conditioned GPsNN outperforms the unconditioned version. Additionally, we illustrate the utility of this pathwise conditioning method by applying it to the GPsNN to solve a differential equation. The results indicate that the pathwise conditioned GPsNN achieves higher accuracy than the unconditioned model. Finally, we show that the pathwise conditioned GPsNN can be utilized to solve a constrained optimization problem. Numerical examples confirm that the pathwise conditioned GPsNN yields better results compared to the unconditioned GPsNN. This study investigates the wireless connectivity of a ground-air sensor network within a two-dimensional domain. The network comprises $n$ ground sensors distributed uniformly at random, each equipped with a communication range of $r_n$. Additionally, $m_n$ airborne sensors are deployed, each with a range of $R_n$, where the ratio $R_n/r_n$ scales as $n^\alpha$ for some $\alpha \geq 0$. The positions of the airborne sensors are determined by a Poisson point process. The analysis examines the probability that the network is connected, specifically focusing on scenarios where the airborne sensors are positioned near the domain's boundary. Furthermore, we explore the impact of boundary effects on network connectivity and establish a lower bound for the probability of connection. Finally, we outline potential avenues for future research. This work extends the findings of \cite{Bose2010} to networks involving airborne sensors. The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a global scientific initiative designed to investigate fundamental questions regarding neutrino properties, nuclear structure, and electroweak interactions. By utilizing a high-intensity, wide-band beam of accelerator-produced neutrinos directed at a far detector situated 1,300 km away, DUNE will achieve unprecedented precision in measuring neutrino oscillation parameters and CP violation. Beyond these core goals, the experiment will conduct searches for sterile neutrinos, perform geoneutrino measurements, study proton decay, and explore dark matter. This paper outlines the scientific objectives of DUNE, details the proposed experimental setup, and presents the projected sensitivity for each scientific objective. Additionally, it addresses the current status of the project and the anticipated timeline for its completion. DUNE is currently in the construction phase, with a target completion date of 2027. The experiment is supported by an international collaboration of over 3,000 scientists and engineers from more than 30 countries. Funding is provided by the U.S. Department of Energy, the National Science Foundation, the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, and numerous other agencies and institutions worldwide. Top tagging is a critical technique in top quark physics, and machine learning methods are widely employed to identify boosted top quarks. This study examines the performance of the recent top tagger, BoostedTop, and provides an interpretation of its decision-making process. We demonstrate that BoostedTop exhibits a strong dependence on the quark's transverse momentum, a factor that is not explicitly included in the tagger's input features. Furthermore, we show that BoostedTop is highly sensitive to the kinematic properties of the final-state jets, a characteristic that may indicate a lack of robustness. These findings are derived from a detailed analysis of the tagger's behavior using Shapley values. Our results offer valuable insights for future research aimed at developing more effective top taggers. Additionally, we present a new top tagger, BoostedTop2, which is robust against the aforementioned issues and demonstrates superior performance compared to BoostedTop. Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in recent years, particularly in control tasks. However, the high variance inherent in RL algorithms often results in unstable training and suboptimal policies. To address this, we introduce a novel experience replay strategy designed to reduce variance during the training of policy gradient methods. Our approach involves storing multiple copies of the same experience within the replay buffer and sampling them to compute the policy gradient. We provide a theoretical analysis of the variance in these gradient estimates and demonstrate that our method can achieve any desired variance level by adjusting the number of experience copies. Extensive experiments on the MuJoCo benchmark suite confirm that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. We compare two distinct approaches for integrating out fermions in supersymmetric theories: the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula. By applying both methods to the same model, we demonstrate that they yield equivalent results, thereby validating the correctness of the superbosonization formula. Additionally, we examine the nonperturbative aspects of these transformations. Our analysis reveals that while both methods can be extended to include nontrivial fermion masses, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation fails to remain valid when the boson mass vanishes. In contrast, the superbosonization formula maintains its validity even in the absence of boson mass. Consequently, the latter is more suitable for investigating nonperturbative phenomena, such as the confinement-deconfinement phase transition. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the large-$N$ limit of the $O(N)$ model. We show that applying the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to this model leads to an incorrect conclusion regarding the nature of the phase transition. However, utilizing the superbosonization formula correctly identifies the phase transition as being of the first order. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings for the $O(N)$ model in $d=3$ dimensions. Our analysis indicates that the superbosonization formula is applicable in $d=3$, whereas the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is not. This suggests that the nonperturbative effects of the fermion mass are essential for the validity of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation in $d=3$. Finally, we address the implications of these findings for the $O(N)$ model in $d=2$ dimensions. We find that both the superbosonization formula and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation are applicable in this dimension. However, the fermion mass plays a crucial role in the former, whereas it is not essential for the latter. These conclusions are consistent with the known properties of the $O(N)$ model in $d=2$ dimensions. In summary, our findings suggest that the superbosonization formula is a more robust tool for analyzing nonperturbative effects in supersymmetric theories compared to the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. This is because the former can be applied to models with vanishing boson mass, whereas the latter requires a nonzero boson mass to remain valid. We demonstrate that neutrinoless double-beta decay occurring at colliders can be achieved even when neutrinos are Dirac particles, provided they exist in multiple Majorana states. This phenomenon arises from the interference between these Majorana states, which generates an effective mass term. We establish that this decay is suppressed when the interference term vanishes. Furthermore, we show that the production of neutrinoless double-beta decay at colliders is contingent upon the neutrino mass matrix, with the most favorable conditions occurring when the matrix is nearly diagonal. Finally, we present a phenomenological analysis of the neutrinoless double-beta decay rate for a specific set of neutrino parameters. Additionally, we examine the impact of the Majorana phase on the decay rate and demonstrate that it can be constrained through a combination of collider and terrestrial experiments. This study underscores the significance of neutrinoless double-beta decay at colliders as a novel method for investigating the nature of neutrinos. Moreover, it highlights the potential of colliders to explore the neutrino sector across a broad spectrum of energy scales. We introduce a straightforward method for estimating the point spread function (PSF) in coadded images, utilizing only the coaddition weights and the final image itself. This approach is applicable to any coaddition technique, including those that do not explicitly model the PSF. We validate the method's accuracy through simulations and apply it to the Pan-STARRS1 coadded images. The results indicate that the estimated PSF aligns closely with the true PSF, with a maximum discrepancy of 0.002 pixels. This accuracy is sufficient for performing accurate photometry on sources within the Pan-STARRS1 survey. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method can be extended to estimate the coadded PSF for individual point sources. This capability is particularly valuable for photometry in crowded fields, where the PSF is dominated by the target source itself. We illustrate this extension using the Pan-STARRS1 1.3g catalog. In these cases, the estimated PSF closely matches the true PSF, with a maximum difference of 0.003 pixels. This finding confirms that the Pan-STARRS1 1.3g catalog is free from significant crowding effects. Additionally, we show that the proposed method can be adapted to estimate the coadded PSF for extended sources. For these sources, the PSF is defined by a Gaussian function, and the estimated full width at half maximum (FWHM) agrees with the true FWHM to within 0.003 pixels. Finally, we demonstrate that the method can be employed to identify sources with anomalous PSFs, such as those affected by crowding. We successfully detect crowding in the Pan-STARRS1 1.3g catalog, with the fraction of crowded sources in the 1.3g catalog being consistent with prior estimates. The source of this crowding is attributed to the Pan-STARRS1 survey's relatively low angular resolution. We also identify a small number of extended sources with anomalous PSFs, which are likely due to the survey's limited depth. Overall, the Pan-STARRS1 1.3g catalog exhibits minimal crowding effects, and the PSF of each source can be accurately estimated using the proposed method. This enables the Pan-STARRS1 survey to achieve its goal of providing a uniform, high-quality photometric catalog. This study examines the fracture toughness of brittle, brittle-ductile, and ductile materials through the lens of linear elasticity and dislocation theory. For brittle solids, we derive the stress intensity factor for a crack within a linearly elastic medium subjected to a point force, a result that aligns with the Green's function approach. In the context of ductile materials, we calculate the stress field around a dislocation in an elastically anisotropic crystal, a derivation that extends the work of Hirth and Lothe. Finally, we address a mixed-bonded material by combining the methodologies from the preceding sections. These findings offer a comprehensive framework for understanding fracture toughness across various material types. The paper concludes with a discussion of the results and their potential applications. The derived estimate demonstrates that the $L^\infty$-norm of the solution remains bounded by a constant multiplied by the sum of the initial data's norm and the norm of the source term. Furthermore, this result extends the methodology previously employed by the author in deriving analogous estimates for the Schrödinger equation. Finally, the paper concludes with an analysis of the implications of this estimate for the Navier-Stokes equations. We introduce a classical verification method for quantum computations that runs in linear time, thereby surpassing the quadratic complexity of earlier approaches. This technique is applicable to any quantum circuit where the number of qubits does not exceed the number of gates. The core of our approach involves a classical verifier that instructs quantum provers to execute a randomly selected subset of gates, while the verifier directly implements the remaining gates. By comparing the joint output distribution of the provers against the expected results, the verifier can identify any prover attempting to deviate from the protocol with a probability of at least $1/2$. Furthermore, we establish a corresponding quantum protocol for the verifier, enabling a quantum verifier to confirm the correctness of a quantum computation in linear time. This advancement is particularly significant for verifying the outputs of large-scale quantum computers. Our findings are derived from a novel analysis of the "diamond norm" distance between quantum channels, which quantifies the maximum distinguishability between two channels when applied to any input state. We demonstrate that this distance can be estimated within linear time. Additionally, we present a new classical algorithm for calculating the diamond norm distance between any two quantum channels, which operates in time proportional to the square of the input dimension. This represents an exponential improvement over the previously best-known complexity. Our algorithm is based on a new characterization of the diamond norm distance, which we believe will have broader applications in quantum information theory. Finally, we outline several extensions of our results, including the ability to verify quantum computations with an arbitrary number of gates in time linear to the gate count, and the verification of quantum circuits with multiple inputs and outputs in time linear to the sum of their dimensions. These generalizations are achieved through the application of our primary result to a specific class of quantum channels. We anticipate that these findings will facilitate the practical verification of quantum computations in real-world applications. The code for our algorithms is publicly accessible on GitHub. We hope that our work will inspire further research into the efficient verification of quantum computations. In conclusion, our results demonstrate that the verification of quantum computations is a feasible task that can be accomplished in linear time. This study introduces a new approach to modeling the geometry of living cells using implicit neural representations. We demonstrate that these representations are highly effective for generating realistic cell shapes and can be trained exclusively on 2D or 3D segmentation masks. Our method employs a multi-scale architecture to capture both local and global shape details, while a novel training strategy ensures that generated outputs remain diverse and morphologically plausible. Furthermore, we show that the trained models can infer cell age from shape data and perform in silico drug screening. Stellar activity significantly impacts the interpretation of exoplanet atmospheres, yet its influence on low-resolution transit spectroscopy remains poorly understood. This study utilizes the HARPS-N instrument to observe the active M1.5V star GJ 1151, which hosts the exoplanet GJ 1151 b. By analyzing the star's spectrum during both out-of-transit and in-transit phases, we measured the depth of the Ca II H&K emission lines. We then compared these measurements with the planet's radius to determine if the planet's atmosphere could be responsible for the observed spectral features. Our results indicate that the planet's atmosphere cannot account for the observed emission lines, confirming that stellar activity is the primary source of the signal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that high-resolution spectroscopy effectively mitigates the effects of stellar activity, thereby enabling the detection of exoplanet atmospheres around active M dwarfs. This finding is crucial for the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope mission. Additionally, we present a new method for characterizing the variability of the stellar chromosphere, which can be applied to any active M dwarf. This approach involves measuring the ratio of the Ca II H&K emission line depth to the continuum depth during in-transit and out-of-transit observations. We applied this technique to GJ 1151 and compared it with the variability of the star's chromospheric emission. Our analysis reveals that the chromosphere of GJ 1151 exhibits a distinct pattern of variability, characterized by a gradual increase in activity over a period of several days. This variability pattern is likely driven by the rotation of active regions across the stellar surface. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for future observations of exoplanets orbiting active M dwarfs. We conclude that high-resolution spectroscopy is essential for mitigating the effects of stellar activity, and that the variability of the chromosphere can be characterized using the proposed method. These insights are vital for the James Webb Space Telescope mission, which aims to study the atmospheres of exoplanets around M dwarfs. By employing high-resolution spectroscopy, researchers can effectively filter out the noise caused by stellar activity, thereby facilitating the detection of exoplanet atmospheres around these active stars. This study examines the locomotion of the centipede *Scutigera coleoptrata* across a range of speeds, from slow progression to rapid escapes. We demonstrate that these animals employ a consistent swimming strategy, utilizing their legs to generate thrust through water displacement. By analyzing the relationship between swimming speed and the frequency of leg movements, we find that the animal's mass plays a critical role in determining the kinematics of its limbs. Furthermore, we show that the centipede's ability to maneuver around obstacles is constrained by its swimming speed. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the mechanics behind the centipede's water surface locomotion. Additionally, our results provide a framework for developing bio-inspired micro-robots capable of traversing water surfaces. This study examines the propagation of dispersive tsunamis generated by asteroid impacts, utilizing a fully nonlinear, fully dispersive wave model. The primary objective is to develop a simulation framework capable of handling the extreme variations in water depth and wave amplitude characteristic of these events. To achieve this, we employ a hybrid numerical approach that integrates the finite element method with the finite volume method. This technique utilizes a sequence of meshes featuring overlapping regions of varying resolution, where the numerical solution is computed across all levels and adaptively transferred between them. The resulting framework is designed to accurately capture the physics of dispersive tsunami propagation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the method effectively manages the severe depth and amplitude contrasts inherent to the problem, while the finite element component ensures the simulation of dispersive effects. Furthermore, the approach exhibits optimal convergence rates and maintains stability even when the mesh transition is abrupt. These findings indicate that the proposed framework is well-suited for simulating the propagation of tsunamis resulting from asteroid impacts. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's potential applications in other fields. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKoch/AdaptiveHybridFEMFVM.
