Our findings indicate that these methods are effective for image recognition tasks involving different architectures and datasets. Furthermore, we observed that these techniques are particularly advantageous when the source and target datasets differ significantly. Finally, we demonstrate that these approaches can be seamlessly integrated into standard deep neural network training workflows. This paper investigates the count of arcs within the affine plane $\mathbb F_q^2$. This wordless proof demonstrates that a regular triangular grid with $n$ vertices per side contains $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for learning on graph-structured data, yet their black-box nature hinders the ability to understand the features driving predictions. This study introduces PGExplainer, a parameterized explainer designed to generate explanations for GNN predictions. The method operates by assigning importance scores to graph nodes and edges, thereby highlighting the specific features responsible for each prediction. To achieve this, PGExplainer trains a parameterized surrogate model that approximates the GNN's output. The surrogate is optimized to minimize the discrepancy between itself and the original GNN while simultaneously maximizing the informativeness of the generated explanations. We evaluate the approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that it produces highly accurate explanations. Furthermore, the method scales effectively to large graphs and supports various GNN architectures. Our results indicate that PGExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art explainers, which were not specifically tailored for GNNs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ailab-cn/pgexplainer. We conducted a substructure analysis of the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 using X-ray data from the Chandra and XMM-Newton observatories, alongside optical data from the SDSS and the VST. The simulation tracks the temporal evolution of both communicative competence and social cohesion. Results indicate that migration significantly accelerates the system's convergence toward a linguistically coherent state. The paper concludes by discussing the model's implications for understanding the evolution of language and social structures. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a promising method for solving inverse problems in science and engineering. However, their practical application is often hindered by slow convergence and the inability to converge to the correct solution due to spectral bias. This study demonstrates that momentum optimization can mitigate spectral bias in PINNs. We validate this finding through both numerical experiments and a theoretical analysis of the gradient flow associated with the time-discretized momentum optimization of PINNs. Our results indicate that this approach can converge to the true solution for both linear and nonlinear inverse problems. Furthermore, we show that the convergence rate of momentum methods is superior to that of standard gradient descent. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that momentum methods achieve faster convergence compared to gradient descent. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Momentum-PINNs. This study examines the stability of a coupled wave system featuring one undamped wave and the other wave subject to locally applied Kelvin-Voigt damping. The undamped wave is categorized into two groups: those sharing the same Dirichlet boundary conditions as the damped wave, and those with distinct boundary conditions. By employing the Fourier transform method, we establish exponential stability for the first group and polynomial stability for the second. Furthermore, we derive the optimal decay rate for the system when the coupling term is linear. Finally, we present a counterexample to demonstrate that exponential stability cannot be guaranteed for this system. Additionally, we provide an example illustrating that polynomial stability may fail if the coupling function is non-constant. These findings extend and complement existing research on the topic. Notably, our analysis does not impose any geometric restrictions on the domain. Finally, we offer an alternative approach to the counterexample, which relies on a different method from the one previously employed. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor J. L. Vazquez. Nonreciprocity is a fundamental concept in optics, defined as the asymmetric transmission of light between two points. This phenomenon is essential for creating robust optical devices, such as isolators and circulators, which are critical for the advancement of quantum information science. This study demonstrates that quantum squeezing can induce nonreciprocity in a linear, time-invariant system. Specifically, we show that an external squeezed vacuum field can produce a unidirectional transmission channel for two-mode squeezed vacuum fields. Furthermore, we illustrate that this quantum squeezing-induced nonreciprocity can be realized using a standard Mach-Zehnder interferometer. These findings offer a new approach to achieving nonreciprocity and provide a promising avenue for developing novel quantum optical devices. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of this phenomenon in quantum communication and quantum information processing. Finally, we outline a feasible experimental implementation of our proposed scheme. Our results establish a foundation for exploring quantum-enhanced optical nonreciprocity. We introduce a novel method for investigating spin-dependent dark matter interactions by utilizing the nuclear spin of $^6$Li. This approach employs a $^6$Li-doped diamond detector to measure the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) frequency shift induced by dark matter. The technique's sensitivity to spin-dependent interactions is comparable to that of nuclear recoil experiments, while offering distinct advantages: it is insensitive to nuclear spin-independent interactions, avoids the need for a cryogenic environment, and enables a direct measurement of the dark matter-nucleon interaction. We demonstrate that a 100-gram detector with a 100-day exposure time can achieve a sensitivity of $10^{-40}$ cm$^3$ for dark matter with a mass of 1 GeV/c$^2$. Furthermore, we outline potential strategies to enhance this sensitivity. This work establishes a foundation for developing a new class of dark matter detectors that probe interactions beyond the standard model. Additionally, the methodology is applicable to other nuclear spin systems, such as $^3$He, $^7$Li, and $^{129}$Xe, which could be implemented in nuclear magnetic resonance experiments. Blind image deblurring aims to recover a sharp image from a blurred one without prior knowledge of the blur kernel. This paper introduces a novel blind deblurring framework utilizing kernel mixtures. The proposed method models the blur kernel as a combination of two components: a Gaussian kernel and a data-driven kernel derived from the input image. By leveraging the statistical properties of the image, this data-driven kernel enhances the accuracy of the blur representation. We introduce the concept of an associative (or Lie) $r$-matrix with coefficients in a graded ring $R$, where the grading is determined by a group $G$. This $r$-matrix is defined as a map from $V$ to $R \otimes \Lambda^2 V$ for any vector space $V$. We demonstrate that such an $r$-matrix naturally generates a $G$-graded Poisson structure on the algebra of functions over $V$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a corresponding Poisson-Lie group structure for any finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra. Finally, we examine the relationship between these $G$-graded Poisson structures and the standard homogeneous associative (or Lie) $r$-matrices. In the specific case where the grading group is $\mathbb{Z}_2$, we provide an explicit description of the associated Poisson structure. Additionally, we outline the construction of a Poisson-Lie group for simple Lie algebras based on this $\mathbb{Z}_2$-grading. This work extends the findings of Bieliavsky, Bonelli, and Ragnisco, who previously addressed the case where the grading group is $\mathbb{Z}$. This paper introduces natural Hoare logic, a formal framework designed for verifying programs based on logical interpretations of natural language specifications. We provide the syntax and semantics for natural language formulas, along with a set of inference rules that constitute the natural Hoare logic. These rules enable the derivation of Hoare triples from natural language formulas, thereby allowing program verification through formal reasoning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting proof system is both sound and complete with respect to the logical form of natural language. Canopus is a resilient, distributed, and synchronous system designed for stateless services, ensuring that all replicas consistently execute the same requests in the correct order. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus capable of tolerating Byzantine faults. The primary innovation is a new broadcast primitive that leverages the synchronous network model to deliver messages to honest participants, even in the presence of Byzantine failures. This mechanism is integrated into the request ordering protocol to guarantee that all honest replicas process requests in an identical sequence. We provide a formal proof demonstrating that RCanopus maintains safety and liveness under Byzantine faults, and we present a prototype implementation of the system. Our experimental results indicate that RCanopus achieves performance comparable to Canopus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RCanopus outperforms other resilient distributed systems, such as PBFT and HotStuff, by utilizing the synchronous network assumption. Finally, we illustrate that RCanopus can be deployed in real-world scenarios, including the Internet, by leveraging the concept of "resilient domains." We have implemented a prototype of RCanopus and deployed it on the Internet to validate this approach. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Resilient-Systems-Lab/RCanopus. This study examines cholesterol's impact on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers using molecular dynamics simulations. We analyze how the modulus varies with cholesterol concentration and compare our findings to existing experimental and simulation data. Our results indicate that cholesterol enhances the bending modulus at low concentrations, peaking at approximately 20 mol%, before causing a decline at higher levels. This decrease is attributed to the formation of cholesterol crystals, which introduce defects and reduce the overall modulus. Additionally, we demonstrate that the standard simulation technique for calculating the bending modulus can be adapted to measure the modulus of a single lipid. Finally, we show that the standard method yields identical results when applied to a single lipid, confirming its validity for both bulk and single-component systems. These insights provide a clearer understanding of cholesterol's role in membrane mechanics and establish a robust framework for future research. This study examines the loop quantum cosmological model derived from the ADM Hamiltonian. The resulting model is classical and can be viewed as a simplified version of the loop quantum cosmological model based on the Thiemann Hamiltonian. We derive the quantum version of this model and demonstrate that it yields the same quantum cosmological equation as the Thiemann-based approach. Furthermore, we show that the quantum cosmological equation for this simplified model can be obtained directly from the Thiemann-based model by taking the limit where the holonomy parameter approaches zero. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings. These results suggest that the specific form of the quantum constraint is not the primary factor in generating the quantum cosmological equation; rather, the critical element is the modification of the classical Hamiltonian constraint. Consequently, the loop quantum cosmological model derived from the ADM Hamiltonian may offer a more straightforward path to quantizing gravity. Additionally, the ADM Hamiltonian is significantly simpler than the Thiemann Hamiltonian, making the loop quantum cosmological model based on it easier to handle. This simplicity could facilitate the development of a more realistic loop quantum cosmological model. Ultimately, the ADM Hamiltonian may serve as a more effective starting point for quantizing gravity. These conclusions are supported by the fact that the ADM Hamiltonian is the most fundamental representation of the Hamiltonian constraint in general relativity. Finally, we note that the loop quantum cosmological model based on the ADM Hamiltonian can be derived directly from the ADM Hamiltonian without requiring the Thiemann trick. This indicates that the Thiemann trick is unnecessary for constructing the loop quantum cosmological model. This study presents a catalog of the 16 most energetic cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory during the initial phase of Phase I operations, spanning from 2004 to 2010. The analysis covers events with energies exceeding 100 EeV, including the two most energetic recorded to date. For each event, we provide the primary observational data, specifically the energy, zenith angle, and arrival direction. Additionally, we examine the energy distribution of these ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and compare the measured flux against various theoretical models. The results indicate that the UHECR flux aligns with the predictions of the Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin (GZK) cutoff. Furthermore, the data suggest a potential correlation between UHECR arrival directions and nearby active galactic nuclei (AGNs) at redshifts below 0.05, although this correlation is not statistically significant. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the origin of UHECRs. The complete catalog is accessible via the Auger Science Data Center (ASDC) at http://www.auger.org/science. Deep object detectors are widely used in computer vision, yet their inability to quantify prediction uncertainty hinders their deployment in safety-critical fields like autonomous driving. This paper introduces BayesOD, a Bayesian framework designed to estimate uncertainty in deep object detectors. By employing a Bayesian perspective, BayesOD offers a unified approach to uncertainty estimation that is both principled and generalizable. Specifically, it utilizes a Bayesian neural network to model the uncertainty of object locations and utilizes Monte Carlo (MC) dropout to assess the uncertainty of object categories. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness on the COCO dataset using the ResNet50 detector, showing that BayesOD significantly outperforms existing methods in both location and category uncertainty estimation. Furthermore, we illustrate its utility in two key applications: enhancing the robustness of object detectors against adversarial attacks and enabling the automatic removal of unreliable predictions. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems, yet it remains a difficult challenge. This paper introduces a new approach for predicting traffic flow on road segments by utilizing traffic moving snippets. These snippets are generated from floating car data and capture the spatiotemporal evolution of traffic conditions. To forecast the future state of a snippet, we employ a graph convolutional network (GCN) to extract spatiotemporal features and a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to predict the next state. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we validate the approach's effectiveness through an ablation study and analyze the model's performance across various road types. We introduce a generalization of rewriting systems to 2-functors within a 2-category, designed to ensure finite coherence proofs for any 2-pseudonatural transformation. This approach is applied to derive novel coherence results for symmetric monoidal categories and to address the coherence problem for braided monoidal categories. Our methodology relies on a technique termed "diagrammatic rewriting," which employs a 2-functor to translate 2-dimensional diagrams into algebraic structures. This process transforms the challenge of diagrammatic coherence into a more manageable algebraic coherence problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method extends to any 2-functor mapping into a 2-category where every object possesses an inverse. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background on rewriting systems and their application to strict monoidal categories. Section 3 defines diagrammatic rewriting and establishes its relationship with standard rewriting systems. Section 4 presents the primary findings, including a generalization of the finite coherence theorem and the application of diagrammatic rewriting to solve coherence issues for braided monoidal categories. Finally, Section 5 outlines several open questions and potential future research directions. This work builds upon the author's PhD thesis, with the original research conducted in 2019. The thesis was subsequently updated in 2021 to incorporate the finite coherence theorem and to apply these findings to braided monoidal categories. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to segment the hippocampus in 3D T1-weighted MRI scans from both healthy individuals and patients with Alzheimer's disease or epilepsy. The approach employs a multi-stage strategy utilizing three distinct Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to address the challenges of hippocampal segmentation in clinical settings. The initial stage involves a U-Net architecture trained to classify voxels as either hippocampus or non-hippocampus. The subsequent stage utilizes a U-Net to predict the hippocampus' 3D orientation. Finally, a U-Net is trained to estimate the hippocampus' 3D volume. The framework was evaluated on two independent datasets: the ADNI and the ILSE-EPILAB. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques. We examine the interferometric single-photon pigeonhole effect, which occurs when a photon is injected into a multi-mode system and subsequently detected in only a subset of those modes. This phenomenon is investigated using both classical and quantum frameworks. In the classical approach, the effect is analyzed through the lens of the optical field's Wigner function. In the quantum approach, it is modeled by restricting the system's Hilbert space to a subspace spanned by a few transversal modes. Our findings indicate that the pigeonhole effect is more pronounced in the quantum scenario, where the probability of the effect scales as $1/N$ for $N$ input modes, compared to the classical scenario, where it scales as $1/\sqrt{N}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the quantum pigeonhole effect can be utilized to achieve a higher success rate in quantum state transfer. Finally, we explore the potential applications of this effect in quantum computing and communication. These results offer valuable insights for the design of quantum state transfer protocols and quantum optical devices. Additionally, our study provides a deeper understanding of the fundamental differences between classical and quantum physics. This study presents a Monte Carlo simulation designed to determine the radiation environment for protons trapped in low Earth orbit (LEO). The model incorporates the geomagnetic field, the atmosphere, and the outer Van Allen radiation belt. Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) have emerged as a prominent deep learning architecture for processing graph-structured data, yet their internal mechanisms remain opaque, hindering the development of more effective models. This paper introduces a novel DGNN architecture designed to enhance both performance and interpretability. We first identify a global pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton within existing DGNNs, which we demonstrate is suboptimal. To address this, we propose a new global shrinkage skeleton that eliminates this bottleneck. Furthermore, we introduce a topology link rewiring mechanism to establish more direct connections between graph nodes and network layers, thereby improving information flow. Experimental results on graph classification and node classification tasks confirm that our proposed architecture achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art models. The matrix completion problem involves reconstructing a low-rank matrix from a subset of observed entries. This paper introduces the first differentially private algorithm for low-rank matrix completion, achieving a sample complexity that is nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors. The proposed method combines the Laplace and Huber mechanisms to ensure privacy. We demonstrate that the algorithm's output is differentially private and that the resulting reconstruction error is nearly optimal within logarithmic terms. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the sample complexity for any differentially private matrix completion algorithm, proving that our approach is nearly optimal. Finally, we empirically validate the performance of our method through numerical experiments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/DP-Matrix-Completion.

We introduce a unified model that describes the extinction, emission, and polarization of light caused by dust in the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM). This model integrates the Astrodust+ framework for dust extinction with the Polarized Atomic Hydrogen Emission (PAH) model for polarized emission. The Astrodust+PAH model successfully replicates the observed correlations among the total-to-selective extinction ratio ($R_V$), the ratio of polarized to total emission at 100 $\mu$m, and the ratio of polarized to total emission at 2175 \AA. Furthermore, it accurately reproduces the correlation between $R_V$ and the ratio of emission at 2175 \AA to emission at 100 $\mu$m. The model also accounts for the variation in the ratio of polarized emission at 2175 \AA to emission at 100 $\mu$m across different Galactic longitudes. Additionally, Astrodust+PAH generates realistic predictions for the polarization fraction and position angle of dust emission at 100 $\mu$m, as well as the polarization angle of dust emission at 2175 \AA. Finally, the model predicts that the polarization angle of dust emission at 2175 \AA is approximately 90 degrees offset from the polarization angle of dust extinction. We report the detection of a giant planet within the disk surrounding the very low-mass star CIDA 1, a system previously identified as a candidate for the lowest mass ratio between a star and its companion. By analyzing ALMA 1.3 mm continuum data, we identified a ring-like structure with a radius of 100 au and a peak flux density of 0.25 mJy. The planet is hypothesized to be responsible for the inner edge of this ring, which aligns with the gap observed in the gas disk. We estimated the planet's mass to be 1.5–2.5 Jupiter masses, derived from the disk's surface density profile and the planet's Hill radius. This mass estimate is consistent with the planet's ability to clear a gap in the gas disk. Additionally, we determined the planet's orbital period to be 1000–1500 years. This system represents the second known case of a giant planet orbiting a very low-mass star, following the discovery of GQ Lup b. The presence of this planet suggests that giant planets can form around very low-mass stars, implying that the minimum stellar mass required for giant planet formation is lower than previously believed. Furthermore, the planet's mass falls within the range of 1–10 Jupiter masses, a regime where the transition between giant planets and brown dwarfs remains uncertain. Consequently, this system offers a unique opportunity to investigate the nature of the lower mass boundary for brown dwarfs. Finally, the planet's mass is comparable to that of brown dwarfs, indicating that brown dwarfs may also be able to carve gaps in protoplanetary disks. This study underscores the necessity of observing disks around very low-mass stars to better understand the formation mechanisms of both giant planets and brown dwarfs.

This paper examines the Most Clicks problem, which involves determining the sequence of maximum length that solves a specific Lights Out puzzle. We establish that for any Lights Out game, a solution of maximum length is guaranteed to be unique. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Most Clicks problem is NP-hard across all grid sizes, with the exception of 2xN grids where N is at least 3. In these 2xN cases, we present an algorithm with O(N) time complexity to compute the length of the longest solution. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the Most Clicks problem and the Hamiltonian path problem within directed graphs. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of our algorithm. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robertk1998/most-clicks. The accompanying video, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222, illustrates the algorithm's execution on a 2x3 grid. The author acknowledges that the problem's name is somewhat misleading, as it does not require finding the longest solution but rather the longest solution corresponding to a specific linear recurrence. Consequently, the term "linear recurrence" would be a more accurate designation. The author also notes that the problem is trivial for 1xN grids, where the longest solution is simply the sequence of all 1s. However, the author remains uncertain whether this triviality extends to other grid dimensions. The author welcomes any corrections or suggestions. Thank you. Robert K. This study introduces a new variational segmentation framework that integrates image restoration techniques to enhance segmentation accuracy. The proposed model incorporates a data fidelity term grounded in image restoration principles, specifically leveraging total variation (TV) denoising and deblurring methods. By utilizing the proximal operator of this fidelity term, the paper derives an optimization algorithm that efficiently solves the resulting energy minimization problem. Furthermore, the results indicate that the proposed method is particularly well-suited for applications involving noisy or blurred images. Abstract interpretation is a static analysis technique that operates through two primary phases: an ascending phase, which computes the least fixed point, and a descending phase, which calculates the greatest fixed point. Although these phases are theoretically independent, current algorithms typically execute them sequentially. This paper introduces a novel abstract interpretation algorithm that integrates both phases into a single, unified process. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by applying it to the static analysis of C programs. Furthermore, we provide experimental results comparing our approach against existing algorithms. Our findings indicate that the proposed algorithm achieves performance comparable to or superior to that of current state-of-the-art methods. This paper introduces a novel framework for fair graph representation learning, designed to address biases inherent in graph data. We propose the concept of neighborhood fairness, which ensures that the distribution of sensitive attributes remains consistent across different neighborhoods within a graph. To operationalize this, we develop a framework called Localized Neighborhood Fairness (LNF), which integrates neighborhood fairness constraints into a graph neural network (GNN) learning process. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that LNF can eliminate neighborhood bias in GNNs. Furthermore, we present an efficient algorithm to solve the LNF problem, which involves learning graph representations while simultaneously identifying and removing biased edges. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of our proposed framework. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/LNF.

This study examines kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions, specifically those involving one or two substrates, and develops iterative numerical methods to solve the associated population balance equations. The proposed approach is demonstrated using two specific cases: the reversible Michaelis-Menten reaction and a reversible enzyme reaction with two substrates. The analysis focuses on scenarios where the initial enzyme state is arbitrary, though it is noted that the method converges to the correct solution when the initial enzyme distribution is uniform. Furthermore, the results indicate that the iterative scheme remains stable even in the presence of numerical errors. Finally, the paper presents several illustrative examples. Notably, the iterative solution for the reversible Michaelis-Menten reaction successfully recovers the known analytical solution. Additionally, the numerical results for the reversible enzyme reaction with two substrates align with previously reported findings. Ultimately, the proposed iterative method is shown to be effective for solving population balance equations in reversible enzyme reactions. However, it is important to acknowledge that the method's efficiency may be compromised when the reaction rate constants are of vastly different orders of magnitude. In such cases, the initial enzyme distribution must be carefully selected to ensure rapid convergence to the correct solution. This requirement is particularly critical when the reaction involves two substrates. Finally, the study concludes that the iterative scheme is applicable to a broader range of reversible enzyme reactions, including those with multiple substrates and products, as well as those exhibiting cooperativity. The paper also provides examples of such reactions. The authors believe this work will be valuable for researchers engaged in the numerical analysis of population balance equations. Furthermore, the authors anticipate that the findings will contribute to the development of efficient numerical methods for solving population balance equations in general. We present a path integral formulation for the steady-state density matrix of a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to both quantum and classical driving forces, solved via the Metropolis algorithm. This approach enables the calculation of the steady-state wave function, from which all relevant physical properties can be derived. The method's validity is confirmed by comparing our results with those obtained from the quantum regression theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the quantum and classical Fokker-Planck equations yield identical solutions for the steady-state density matrix when the system is driven by a white noise source. Finally, we show that the Metropolis algorithm can be extended to handle arbitrary quantum systems. These findings indicate that the proposed method is both efficient and accurate for investigating the steady states of quantum harmonic oscillators and broader quantum systems. Additionally, we discuss the method's potential applications in quantum thermodynamics. This work is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11974290). Item recommendation is a core function of online platforms, and its performance is significantly influenced by the quality of data. User reviews serve as valuable data sources that can enhance recommendation systems. However, existing review-based methods often overlook the impact of sentiment, which is crucial for understanding review content. To address this limitation, we introduce the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), designed to integrate sentiment information into recommendation models. SIFN employs a multi-layer architecture that progressively fuses sentiment-aware user and item representations. Additionally, it utilizes a sentiment-aware attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the importance of different sentiment aspects within the review data. Experimental results demonstrate that SIFN effectively leverages sentiment information to improve recommendation performance. Furthermore, our analysis of the learned sentiment representations reveals that the model successfully captures the semantic meaning of reviews. Data sparsity remains a significant challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for Arabic, a problem that is exacerbated when dealing with Arabic-English code-switched text. This study examines the efficacy of lexical replacements as a data augmentation strategy for such text. We evaluate three approaches: (1) substituting words with their most frequent synonyms, (2) replacing words with their least frequent synonyms, and (3) swapping words with their lemma forms. Our findings indicate that the third approach—replacing words with their lemmas—yields the most promising results. We validate this conclusion through experiments on two tasks: code-switched machine translation and code-switched text classification. Additionally, we explore the potential of using word embeddings to identify semantically similar words for augmentation purposes. Hexahedral meshes are essential for various computational tasks, including computer graphics, computer-aided design, and finite element analysis. However, these meshes often contain topological errors, such as invalid hexahedra, which hinder their utility. This paper introduces a new algorithm capable of untangling such meshes. The method relies on a novel class of local transformations known as "tets," which convert invalid hexahedra into tetrahedra. By applying a sequence of these tets, the algorithm successfully untangles the mesh. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach can achieve up to 58 tets per hexahedron, representing a significant improvement over previous methods. Furthermore, the technique is versatile enough to handle diverse mesh types, including those with holes, self-intersections, and degenerate hexahedra. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/HexTangle/HexTangle. Relation extraction (RE) involves identifying the relationships between entities within a given text. Although numerous methods have been developed for this task, they often struggle with the challenge of co-occurrence, where multiple entities appear together in the same sentence. To address this, we introduce a new RE framework that integrates knowledge graph link prediction. This approach utilizes knowledge graphs to resolve co-occurrence issues and enhance RE performance. Specifically, the model first identifies all entity pairs within a sentence, then calculates the probability of their relationship by aggregging contextual information from the text. Finally, it incorporates link prediction scores from the knowledge graph to refine the RE outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the RE-TK and TKG-RE datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/KPLP. Additionally, we have established a new knowledge graph benchmark, the TKG-RE dataset, which can be downloaded from https://github.com/ChenYi2000/KPLP/tree/main/TKG-RE. This paper introduces a novel analytical delay model for CMOS inverters that utilizes the inverter's voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) to determine delay. The model employs a piecewise linear approximation of the inverter's output voltage response, derived from the VTC, to calculate delay values. By fitting the VTC with straight lines, the model ensures linearity, which simplifies delay computation. Furthermore, the proposed method is implemented in Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox to streamline the process of generating the piecewise linear VTC approximation. The study demonstrates that this approach yields highly accurate delay estimates with minimal computational effort. Additionally, the model's accuracy is validated through comparison with SPICE simulations. The results indicate that the proposed model achieves an average error of less than 1% relative to SPICE data. Consequently, this method is particularly well-suited for the early stages of the design flow, where rapid delay estimation is essential. The paper also includes Matlab code for the implementation, which can be accessed via the provided link. The code is designed to be easily adaptable for use in other design environments. The ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is hypothesized to organize animacy based on shared visual features, yet this claim remains unverified. To address this, we utilized a large-scale dataset of natural images paired with human neural recordings from VTC. We employed a novel image classification method to identify visual features that align with the population-level animacy representation within the cortex. Our findings indicate that the animacy representation in VTC is not driven by common visual features, contradicting the prevailing hypothesis. Instead, the data supports the view that animacy is organized along a continuous spectrum rather than as a binary distinction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the visual features associated with animacy in VTC are more strongly linked to the continuous spectrum of animacy than to the binary categorization. These results offer a new perspective on the nature of animacy representation in the ventral temporal cortex. Additionally, our methodology for extracting population-level representations from neural data may prove valuable for investigating other complex cognitive representations. Finally, we provide an open-source Python package to facilitate the replication of our results. The code is available at https://github.com/Neuroscience-ML/animacy-VTC. This study introduces a structure-preserving filter designed for finite element simulations in multiple dimensions. The method relies on a variational framework utilizing a convex objective function, which is efficiently minimized through the alternating direction method of multipliers. The filter's performance is validated across various 2D and 3D test cases, demonstrating its robustness and effectiveness in smoothing finite element data. Furthermore, the approach is applied to postprocess results from a phase-field simulation modeling the solidification of a binary alloy. The proposed technique offers a significant advantage over traditional filters by eliminating the need for manual parameter tuning, as the variational approach automatically determines optimal smoothing parameters. Additionally, the method exhibits data-independent behavior, ensuring consistent performance across different datasets. The implementation is accessible via the open-source software platform FEniCS. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. The source code is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10000000. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) are frequently observed in the hard X-ray band of black hole X-ray binaries (BHXBs) during the hard-intermediate state (HIS). This study utilizes the Insight-HXMT to track the evolution of type-C QPOs in the BHXB MAXI J1535-571, which is currently in the HIS. Our analysis reveals that the type-C QPO in MAXI J1535-571 exhibits a low frequency of 0.5–1.0 Hz, with its fractional root mean square (RMS) amplitude peaking at approximately 10% during the outburst. We observed a strong anti-correlation between the type-C QPO frequency and the hard X-ray flux, alongside a positive correlation between the type-C QPO fractional RMS and the hard X-ray flux. Furthermore, the type-C QPO frequency displays a positive correlation with the power spectral density (PSD) break frequency. These findings align with the results from MAXI J1348-63. Additionally, we identified a new correlation between the type-C QPO fractional RMS and the fractional RMS of the 2–4 keV band, which is consistent with observations of MAXI J1348-63. Finally, the evolution of the type-C QPO in MAXI J1535-571 mirrors that of MAXI J1348-63, suggesting that both systems may share similar accretion disk structures. These results are consistent with the standard accretion disk instability model. However, the observed correlations between the type-C QPO frequency, PSD break frequency, and hard X-ray flux contradict the predictions of the relativistic accretion disk instability model. Consequently, we propose that the type-C QPO in MAXI J1535-571 may originate from the accretion disk. Furthermore, the type-C QPO fractional RMS in MAXI J1535-571 is significantly lower than that of MAXI J1348-63, indicating that the two systems likely possess different accretion disk structures. We propose Transfer Empowerment (TE), a social intrinsic motivation designed to guide agents toward states where their partners are likely to take desired actions. Furthermore, we show that TE offers a straightforward and effective approach for learning to predict partners' actions. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of TE across various MARL tasks, including a complex, realistic scenario involving a multi-agent soccer game. This paper provides an overview of Lie 2-algebras, also known as categorical Lie algebras. We begin by reviewing the standard definition of a Lie 2-algebra and then examine its connection to Lie algebroids. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Lie 2-algebras are equivalent to strict Lie 2-groups acting on vector spaces. Finally, we introduce the concept of a representation of a Lie 2-algebra and establish its relationship with representations of strict Lie 2-groups. Additionally, we define representations of Lie 2-algebras as categories equipped with a functorial action. We illustrate this theory with examples, including the Lie 2-algebra associated with a Lie algebroid and the standard Lie 2-algebra of a Lie group. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. This work serves as a foundation for the author's Master's thesis, which is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01001. The current version incorporates several corrections and enhancements compared to the thesis. Specifically, the definition of a representation of a Lie 2-algebra has been refined, and the equivalence between representations of Lie 2-algebras and representations of strict Lie 2-groups has been strengthened. Furthermore, the discussion regarding the adjoint representation has been expanded. Finally, the paper now includes a more comprehensive list of references. The primary distinction between this version and the thesis lies in the inclusion of a more extensive bibliography. This study examines the bias inherent in the Inferred Measurement (IM) technique used for solar vector magnetic field data. We demonstrate that the bias in the IM line-of-sight (LOS) component is directly proportional to the bias in the measured Stokes $Q$ and $U$ components. Furthermore, we establish that the IM method yields unbiased results only when the magnetic field is weak and the line-of-sight angle remains small. To address this bias, we introduce a novel approach that combines the Inferred Measurement (IM) and Inversion Measurement (InvM) methods. This new technique effectively eliminates the bias in the IM LOS component while maintaining high sensitivity for strong magnetic fields. Additionally, we show that the proposed method significantly reduces noise in strong magnetic fields compared to the InvM method. Finally, we apply this bias-corrected method to real observations from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) to analyze the evolution of magnetic fields in a sunspot group. The results indicate that the magnetic field strength in the sunspot umbra increases over time, whereas the field strength in the penumbra remains relatively stable. These findings align with existing literature. Our proposed method offers a straightforward and effective solution for bias correction in solar vector magnetic field data. The associated Python code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/IM_InvM. This study introduces a novel demand-side management framework designed to optimize energy consumption scheduling and implement instantaneous load billing. Within this system, a central aggregator coordinates the scheduling process, while a billing mechanism ensures that the collective benefits of coordination are fairly distributed among participating consumers. To achieve this, we propose an aggregative game where each consumer's utility function incorporates both scheduling costs and billing expenses. We demonstrate the existence of a scheduling equilibrium and prove that the proposed billing scheme guarantees this equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish the Pareto optimality of this equilibrium and present a distributed algorithm to compute it. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The results indicate that the instantaneous load billing scheme successfully incentivizes consumers to reduce their peak loads, thereby lowering the system's peak load and total billing costs. Additionally, the proposed algorithm enables consumers to determine their optimal schedules in a distributed manner without requiring knowledge of other consumers' schedules or costs. This approach also facilitates the fair distribution of the system's overall benefits among the participants. The effectiveness of the method is further confirmed by comparing the performance of the proposed algorithm against a centralized algorithm. Ultimately, this research offers a new perspective on demand-side management, with potential applications in smart grid operations and energy management systems. The proposed method can be readily adapted to various billing schemes and energy consumption scheduling problems. This study examines the Hawking radiation of charged black strings within Rastall theory, a framework where the conservation of the energy-momentum tensor is contingent upon the value of the Rastall parameter $\eta$. By solving the Klein-Gordon equation using the WKB approximation, we determine the radiation characteristics of these black strings. Our findings indicate that the radiation temperature is influenced by both the Rastall parameter $\eta$ and the Gauss-Bonnet parameter $\lambda$. Furthermore, we observe that the radiation rate diminishes as either $\eta$ or $\lambda$ increases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the area law for the horizon remains valid in this context. Finally, we analyze the stability of charged black strings by investigating the relationship between the change in horizon area and the change in mass. Our results reveal that the stability of the system depends on the specific values of $\eta$ and $\lambda$. Finally, we explore the physical implications of these findings. We establish links between the convergence rates of time averages in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem and the characteristics of spectral measures. Specifically, we demonstrate that the speed of convergence for these averages is intrinsically tied to the regularity of the spectral measure. Furthermore, we derive novel, equivalent formulations of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem that offer greater insight into its convergence rates. These alternative forms are particularly valuable for analyzing systems with non-ergodic dynamics. Finally, we present several applications of these results to the ergodic properties of quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators. Notably, we provide a new, self-contained proof of the absence of singular continuous spectrum in such operators when the Lyapunov exponent is positive. Additionally, we derive new criteria for the singular continuous spectrum in cases where the Lyapunov exponent vanishes. These criteria are demonstrated by the singular continuous spectrum found in the singular spectrum of the almost Mathieu operator under resonance conditions. The proofs rely on a spectral gap condition for the associated fiber Hamiltonians, a concept introduced by Bourgain and Goldstein. This condition enables the reduction of spectral analysis to the study of periodic operators, thereby facilitating the application of various techniques from periodic operator theory. We anticipate that this approach will be applicable to a broad range of other models. Finally, we propose a conjecture regarding the spectral type of quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators, which synthesizes recent findings on singular continuous spectrum and Anderson localization. We demonstrate that this conjecture holds true for the singular spectrum of the almost Mathieu operator when the frequency is of Diophantine type. The proof utilizes the equivalent form of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem to analyze the spectral type of the associated fiber Hamiltonians. This work represents a significant advancement in the spectral theory of quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators. It provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the spectral type of these operators and offers a unified perspective on the spectral types of the almost Mathieu operator, the Fibonacci Hamiltonian, and the Lyapunov exponent. The framework is expected to be applicable to a wide range of other models. The proofs employ a variety of techniques from spectral theory, including the spectral gap condition, the spectral singularities of periodic operators, and the spectral type of periodic operators. We believe that these methods will be useful in the analysis of quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators in general. We introduce a novel approach to detect metal-poor stars using Gaia Blue Photometer/Red Photometer (BP/RP) spectra. This technique relies on a machine learning algorithm that leverages the distinct spectral characteristics of these stars. We applied the method to the Gaia Early Data Release 3 (EDR3) dataset, which includes 1,100,000 stars with BP/RP spectra. Our analysis identified 1,000 metal-poor stars with a [Fe/H] < -2.0, achieving a precision of 99.9% and a recall of 98.5%. The resulting sample exhibits a median [Fe/H] of -2.12 and a median $\log(g)$ of 4.32. Furthermore, we successfully recovered 99.5% of the known metal-poor stars from the APOGEE-2 survey within the Gaia sample. This study demonstrates that the Gaia mission can efficiently identify metal-poor stars, thereby expanding the available sample for future spectroscopic follow-up investigations. The catalog of these stars is accessible via the Gaia archive. Additionally, we provide the code used for the identification process, which can be applied to future Gaia data releases. This study introduces a new dataset and forecasting model for fire season severity, utilizing data from the MODIS active fire detection product. We define fire season severity as the count of active fires occurring during a specific period. Leveraging this dataset, we developed a forecasting model that utilizes severity metrics from the preceding three years to predict severity for the upcoming year. The model's performance is evaluated using the Diebold-Mariano test, which confirms that the proposed model outperforms the naive no-change forecast. Additionally, we assess the model's effectiveness across various spatial scales, including global, continental, and regional levels. Finally, we apply the model to forecast fire season severity for 2022 and 2023. The resulting predictions indicate that 2022 will experience higher severity than 2021 in South America, Africa, and Australia, whereas 2023 is projected to show lower severity compared to 2022 in those same regions. These findings are intended to assist researchers and policymakers in better understanding and mitigating the impacts of wildfires. The complete dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7110000. The accompanying R package, MODISFire, can be installed via the command `devtools::install_github("josephgao/MODISFire")`. Furthermore, the package includes a user-friendly dashboard available at https://josephgao.shinyapps.io/MODISFire/ for visualizing and analyzing the data. The source code for the forecasting model is located in the `forecasting` folder within the MODISFire package. The data utilized in this work was generated or analyzed by the authors using MODIS Fire products from NASA's Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center (LP DAAC), which are distributed by the NASA Earth Observations (NEO) Distributed Active Archive Center (DAAC). The MODIS Fire data is freely accessible at https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/fires/. This study investigates the relationships among various corpus-derived metrics for morphological complexity. We evaluate six distinct measures across three established typological dimensions: morpheme-per-word ratios, the count of morphophonemic features, and the count of phonemes. Our findings indicate that while these measures correlate moderately with one another, they capture different aspects of complexity. Consequently, we recommend that researchers employing such measures to test typological hypotheses clearly specify which dimension their chosen metric aligns with. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric for phonological complexity and demonstrate that it aligns with existing phonological complexity measures. Finally, we illustrate the utility of these findings by applying them to examine the correlation between morphological and phonological complexity. Our results confirm that the correlation between complexity measures is not uniform across all dimensions, thereby challenging the notion that morphological complexity is entirely independent of phonological complexity. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for the debate regarding whether complexity measures reflect the cognitive difficulty of language processing. The paper concludes with a discussion of the broader implications of our results. We investigate gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters, specifically focusing on strong lensing arcs and weak lensing mass maps, to determine the most probable dark matter (DM) profile. Our analysis reveals that the Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) profile, which is typical of cold dark matter (CDM) halos, is disfavored by the data. Instead, we find that a self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) profile, characterized by a shallower slope in the inner region, aligns more closely with observations. This conclusion holds true for both strong and weak lensing analyses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a simple two-component SIDM model, consisting of a massive DM particle and a light mediator, can successfully reproduce the observed mass profiles. This model also accounts for the cusp-core problem in dwarf galaxies and the baryonic feedback effects seen in galaxy disks. Additionally, we show that the mediator mass within this framework can be constrained using lensing data. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for the self-interaction cross section of dark matter. These results suggest that the self-interaction cross section is approximately $0.01\sigma_T m_{DM}/\mathrm{GeV}$, a value consistent with constraints derived from dwarf galaxies and baryonic feedback. Consequently, our findings support the SIDM hypothesis and provide a novel method to constrain the mediator mass. This approach offers a complementary perspective to that of dwarf galaxies, which are sensitive to the inner DM profile, while our study utilizes the outer profile of galaxy clusters. This work represents the first attempt to constrain the mediator mass using galaxy cluster lensing data. Our findings indicate that the mediator mass is likely below $10^{-3}\mathrm{eV}$, a range that remains unconstrained by other methods. This suggests that the mediator is likely a dark photon, which could have significant implications for dark matter annihilation. This study examines the model reduction of a continuous-time stochastic process using only partial state observations. The original process is approximated by a finite-dimensional Markovian reduced model, where the reduced state corresponds to a hidden state estimated via a Kalman-Bucy filter. The paper establishes conditions guaranteeing the convergence of the reduced state's distribution to the original process's distribution, measured by the 2-Wasserstein distance. Furthermore, it analyzes the convergence of the reduced model's output to the original process's observed output, quantified by the mean squared error. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate the theoretical findings. The authors conclude that the proposed method offers a significant advantage over existing model reduction techniques, which typically require full state measurements. Additionally, the approach is applicable to model reduction scenarios where the original process is non-Markovian. The authors' website (https://www.math.tu-berlin.de/~schmalfu/) provides the Python code used for the numerical experiments. The source code is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/maikschmalfu/model_reduction_partial_observations. The Python package implementing the method is named `pyMRPO` and can be installed via pip. The package's source code is hosted at https://github.com/maikschmalfu/pyMRPO. This study addresses the challenge of maximizing expected revenue for a display advertiser within a budget-constrained display auction. We introduce a new adaptive, risk-aware bidding strategy designed to optimize revenue under budget limits. Our approach integrates a novel risk-aware bidding model with an adaptive learning mechanism. The model incorporates both the advertiser's risk tolerance and the predicted click-through rate (CTR) to dynamically adjust bid amounts. Simultaneously, the adaptive learning component continuously refines CTR predictions by analyzing historical bidding and auction data. We evaluate our method against two baselines: a fixed bidding strategy and a model-based strategy that relies solely on predicted CTR. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms the fixed strategy and achieves revenue comparable to the model-based approach. Furthermore, our method exhibits superior robustness when dealing with inaccurate CTR predictions. Finally, we assess the impact of various risk tolerance levels on bidding behavior and revenue outcomes. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/ARAB}. Wigner negativity is a crucial resource for quantum computation and communication, yet its relationship with quantum steering remains unclear. This study investigates that connection by examining the quantum Wigner negativity (WQ) of Wigner functions derived from quantum states. We establish a general theorem demonstrating that the WQ of any bipartite quantum state is at least as high as that of any of its reduced states. This finding offers a novel method for establishing Wigner negativity lower bounds for quantum states. Furthermore, we prove that for any bipartite quantum state, the presence of Wigner negativity in one reduced subsystem implies Wigner negativity in the other. Additionally, we explore the link between quantum steering and Wigner negativity, revealing that the WQ of a bipartite state is at least as great as the Wigner negativity of the Wigner function associated with its unsteerable assemblage. Finally, we present a counterexample to a conjecture by Chaves et al., which posited that the Wigner function of an unsteerable assemblage must be non-negative. This example illustrates that the Wigner negativity of an unsteerable assemblage can be negative, thereby disproving the conjecture. These results offer new perspectives on the interplay between quantum steering and Wigner negativity. The paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews the definitions of quantum steering and Wigner negativity; Section III establishes the theorem regarding the Wigner negativity of bipartite states and their reductions; Section IV addresses the counterexample to the aforementioned conjecture; and Section V concludes the paper. This study presents a secure bound analysis of the six-state quantum key distribution protocol, incorporating privacy amplification via random seeds that lack uniform distribution. The analysis demonstrates that the secure key rate remains unaffected by the non-uniformity of these seeds. Furthermore, the derived secure key rate formula is compared against existing research, and the findings are validated through numerical simulations. These results indicate that the proposed formula is more general and applicable to practical scenarios. Additionally, the research confirms that the secure key rate is independent of the random seed's distribution, thereby offering a more comprehensive theoretical foundation for the secure bound analysis of quantum key distribution systems utilizing non-uniform random seeds in privacy amplification. This insight is particularly valuable for the development of quantum key distribution systems employing random seed generators with non-uniform distributions. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the study's limitations and potential directions for future work. We introduce a diagrammatic approach to model the scattering of multi-photon states within waveguide QED systems. This method is validated by comparing its predictions against those of a straightforward analytical model. Additionally, we utilize the approach to investigate the scattering of two-photon and three-photon states, as well as their correlations, through numerical simulations. Our findings indicate that these states can be scattered with high fidelity, exhibiting distinct behaviors contingent upon the specific coupling configuration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the approach enables the generation of multi-photon states with tailored photon number distributions. These capabilities are anticipated to facilitate the development of novel quantum information processing devices. Spin-dependent (SD) scattering is a primary mechanism for detecting Dark Matter (DM) within the standard framework. However, in the Boosted Dark Matter (BDM) scenario, where DM is accelerated to relativistic velocities, the traditional spin-dependent cross-section becomes inadequate. This paper introduces a novel, model-independent formalism to calculate the differential cross-section for relativistic DM scattering off nucleons. Our approach incorporates the relativistic motion of the nucleon and the full matrix element, while also accounting for the finite size of the nucleon through a generalized form factor. We demonstrate that the BDM spin-dependent cross-section can be enhanced by up to two orders of magnitude compared to the non-relativistic case. Furthermore, we apply this formalism to analyze the BDM scenario using the LUXE experiment, which employs an electron beam to probe the DM-nucleon interaction. We find that the LUXE experiment could achieve sensitivity to BDM with a mass of approximately 10 GeV, reaching an exposure of $10^{21}$ electrons. This capability surpasses the projected LZ limit by roughly two orders of magnitude and exceeds the projected DarkSide-20k limit by about one order of magnitude. Additionally, we show that the LUXE sensitivity can improve by a factor of 10 if the nucleon form factor is optimized. These findings suggest that LUXE has the potential to significantly advance the search for Boosted Dark Matter. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our results for other experimental searches. Our work establishes a formalism that can be applied to any BDM model, offering a substantial boost to the sensitivity of future searches for relativistic Dark Matter. This paper presents Faulhaber's formula for computing the sum of the $k$th powers of the first $n$ natural numbers, alongside the recursive definition of the Bernoulli numbers. It further provides an explicit formula for the Bernoulli numbers that facilitates straightforward calculation. Additionally, the authors offer a Faulhaber-based proof of the inductive formula for the special case where $k=2$. The paper concludes with a discussion of the Faulhaber polynomial's symmetry and its relationship to the Catalan numbers. Finally, the Faulhaber formula is applied to evaluate the sum of the $k$th powers of the first $n$ odd natural numbers. This application demonstrates that the Faulhaber polynomial for odd numbers can be derived from the standard Faulhaber polynomial by adjusting the Bernoulli terms. The authors also present an alternative proof for this result, which utilizes the Faulhaber polynomials for the first $n$ natural numbers and the first $n$ even natural numbers. The paper ends with a discussion of Faulhaber's formula in relation to the Stirling numbers of the first and second kind. The technique is validated through simulations of non-coherent differential detection for CPM signals with minimum energy spectral density. Results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to conventional differential detection with the same differential order, while simultaneously reducing the differential order by a factor of two. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against phase noise, outperforming conventional differential detection in both delay efficiency and overall performance. Finally, the approach is applicable to various CPM signal formats, including those with minimum energy spectral density. The paper concludes by outlining the method's advantages and potential applications. The authors hope this work will inspire further research into delay-efficient non-coherent CPM detection. This study introduces a novel Bayesian inference framework for extreme value analysis, utilizing a reparameterisation of the standard Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT) model. The approach models exceedances as a non-homogeneous Poisson process, where the intensity function is defined by the POT distribution. This method offers two primary benefits: first, it eliminates the necessity for data thinning, thereby fully leveraging the information within the dataset; second, it simplifies the POT distribution's parameterisation, which enhances the stability of Bayesian inference. The proposed method is evaluated through a simulation study and applied to a real-world dataset. Results indicate that the reparameterisation significantly improves the stability of inference, particularly for the shape parameter, while demonstrating only a marginal increase in computational time. Furthermore, the analysis of the real data reveals that the Poisson process model yields superior estimates for the shape parameter compared to the conventional POT approach. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research avenues. This study examines the Equation of State (EoS) of hot QCD matter within small volumes, with a specific focus on the transition region. We analyze the impact of finite volume effects on the EoS using the Polyakov-loop Extended Quark-Meson model, which incorporates dynamical chiral symmetry breaking and confinement. Our results demonstrate that finite volume effects are substantial in small systems, significantly altering the EoS. Furthermore, we investigate how these effects evolve as the system size increases. Finally, we explore the potential for extracting the EoS of small systems from lattice QCD simulations. This research is motivated by recent experimental efforts to measure the EoS of small systems, which could provide critical insights into the QCD phase diagram. Our findings indicate that the EoS of small systems differs markedly from that of the infinite volume limit, a distinction that must be accounted for when interpreting experimental data. Ultimately, this work underscores the necessity of investigating the EoS of small systems to achieve a comprehensive understanding of the QCD phase diagram. This device blocks the Lyman-$\beta$ line and the continuum at wavelengths longer than 1216 \AA, while permitting Lyman-$\alpha$ photons to pass through. Image retrieval is a critical component of digital image management, yet it remains a difficult challenge due to the vast size of image collections and the limitations of current indexing methods. These existing approaches typically rely on either low-level features, which fail to capture semantic meaning, or high-level features, which are costly to generate. This paper introduces a novel indexing method termed "Active Image Indexing," which integrates both low-level and high-level features. The process begins by creating a basic index using low-level features. Subsequently, when a query is received, the system retrieves a subset of images from this basic index and computes their corresponding high-level features. These features are then utilized to rank the retrieved images. Experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid approach outperforms methods relying solely on either low-level or high-level features. Furthermore, the study confirms that the method is scalable, capable of handling large image collections. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abdullah-ali/active-image-indexing. This paper introduces a keyless authentication framework designed for the Gaussian channel. In this approach, the transmitter and receiver utilize a shared secret key for initial authentication, after which the system transitions to a keyless state. During this phase, the transmitter sends a message, and the receiver verifies its authenticity by checking if the message lies within a specific set. The framework's performance is evaluated based on the probability of successful authentication and the key rate required to achieve a target authentication level. We demonstrate that, for a given key rate, the optimal authentication set consists of a Gaussian codebook. Furthermore, we derive an achievable region mapping key rate against successful authentication probability and establish a corresponding converse result. Finally, we compare our findings with the authentication scheme proposed by Liang and Goldsmith (2007). Additionally, we extend the framework to handle messages with length constraints, proving that the optimal authentication set remains a Gaussian codebook in this scenario as well. This result is achieved by applying the same methodology used for messages without length constraints. We also derive the achievable region and converse for messages with length constraints and compare these results with the scheme by Liang and Goldsmith (2007). Finally, we examine the framework's application to the erasure channel. In this context, the optimal authentication set is shown to be a constant-length subcode of a polar code, and we provide the corresponding achievable region and converse. We compare these results with the erasure channel authentication scheme by Liang and Goldsmith (2007). In all cases, the proposed framework outperforms the scheme by Liang and Goldsmith (2007). The paper concludes with a discussion of the framework's limitations and potential future research directions. The results presented herein were previously published in the IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT) 2021. The current version includes a more detailed analysis of the achievability and converse results, as well as an extension of the framework to messages with length constraints. We examine the angular momentum of the quantum vacuum in the presence of a point charge within a uniform magnetic field. Our findings indicate that this angular momentum is non-zero and exhibits a linear relationship with the magnetic field's angular momentum. This linear proportionality persists even in the limit of zero magnetic field, a phenomenon we attribute to the breaking of rotational symmetry by the Landau gauge. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this angular momentum is necessary to satisfy the angular component of the total angular momentum conservation law. Additionally, we explore the implications of this angular momentum for the quantum vacuum in a rotating frame. Finally, we discuss the connection between this angular momentum and the angular momentum of the electromagnetic field surrounding a classical point charge in a magnetic field, as described by the Poynting vector. This classical angular momentum also scales linearly with the magnetic field's angular momentum and remains non-zero even when the magnetic field is absent. We argue that the quantum vacuum angular momentum we calculate is the quantum counterpart to this classical angular momentum. This correspondence is further supported by the fact that both the quantum and classical angular momenta vanish in the Coulomb gauge. The classical angular momentum around a point charge was originally proposed by Jackson and later revisited by various researchers. Our results suggest that the angular momentum of the electromagnetic field around a point charge is not merely a pseudo-momentum but constitutes a genuine angular momentum. Consequently, this classical angular momentum must be included in the total angular momentum of a point charge in a magnetic field. We also note that the angular momentum of the electromagnetic field around a classical point charge in a magnetic field is non-zero even in the Coulomb gauge, a fact that has been debated in the literature. We demonstrate that this apparent contradiction can be resolved by appropriately selecting the gauge function. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the angular momentum of a charged black hole. This proportionality holds true even in the limit of zero black hole angular momentum. This approach leverages the observed acceleration of the primary star, the known mass of the visible companion, and the measured proper motions of both bodies. This study examines the classical problem of determining if a directed acyclic graph (DAG) can be drawn such that all edges follow a specific direction, with a focus on parameterized complexity. We demonstrate that upward planarity is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by the product of the number of vertices and the treewidth of its underlying undirected graph. Furthermore, we establish that the problem remains FPT when parameterized by the number of vertices and the treedepth of the underlying graph. Finally, we prove that both problems are W[1]-hard if parameterized solely by the treewidth or treedepth, respectively, without considering the number of vertices. These findings are derived from a novel characterization of the underlying undirected graph for upward planar DAGs, which we believe holds independent significance. Additionally, we present an algorithm that identifies a biconnected component within an upward planar DAG that lacks an upward planar embedding, running in time $O(n^2 \cdot \text{treewidth}^3 \log \text{treewidth})$. This result relies on the observation that the underlying graph of any upward planar DAG with a specific property is outerplanar. We also provide an algorithm to detect this property in $O(n \cdot \text{treewidth}^2 \log \text{treewidth})$ time. Finally, we extend our findings to the case of upward planar drawings on surfaces. The paper includes a comprehensive survey of existing results and concludes with a discussion of several open questions. While many methods exist for this purpose, most depend on the assumption of independence among units, a condition that is frequently violated in practice. Entrainment, a social phenomenon where individuals subtly mimic the speech patterns of their conversation partners, serves as a key indicator of successful communication. This study introduces a new neural network-based approach to measure entrainment distance, a metric that quantifies the degree of entrainment between conversational partners. The proposed method relies on the hypothesis that the divergence between the acoustic features of two speakers diminishes as entrainment increases. To validate this, we conducted an experiment using the IEMOCAP dataset, which revealed that the proposed entrainment distance effectively captures the behavior of actual conversational partners. Furthermore, we demonstrated that this distance can be utilized to predict the likelihood of successful communication. These findings suggest that the entrainment distance offers a promising avenue for future research into communication success. Additionally, the method is computationally efficient, making it well-suited for real-time applications. Finally, we highlight the method's potential for application in conversational speech technologies, such as virtual assistants. Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is a critical task in video analysis that involves identifying action boundaries and segmenting videos based on temporal actions. While most TAS methods depend on labeled data, unsupervised TAS offers a promising solution for large-scale video datasets where annotations are scarce. This paper introduces Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP), a novel unsupervised TAS framework that leverages the inherent co-occurrence of actions within video clips. SSCAP employs a two-stage pipeline: first, it generates pseudo-labels for action segments using a self-supervised learning approach; second, it trains a deep neural network to perform temporal action segmentation based on these pseudo-labels. Experimental results on the Two-Stage TAS benchmark demonstrate that SSCAP achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised TAS, attaining 60.5% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the THUMOS14 dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/SSCAP. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01209. This study examines the impact of feedback mechanisms on student performance in software testing education. An empirical investigation was conducted involving 120 undergraduate students across three groups: one receiving traditional detailed feedback, another receiving inquiry-based conceptual feedback, and a third serving as a control group with no feedback. The results indicate that both feedback types significantly improved testing skills compared to the no-feedback group. However, the inquiry-based group outperformed the traditional feedback group, demonstrating that conceptual feedback fosters deeper understanding and encourages students to apply their knowledge to novel scenarios. These findings offer valuable insights for software testing educators regarding the most effective pedagogical strategies.
