Domain adaptation is a widely adopted technique for addressing domain shifts, yet most existing approaches require access to both source and target domain data. This paper introduces a novel domain adaptation framework that operates solely with a fixed, pre-trained source model and unlabeled target data, eliminating the need for a source dataset. To achieve this, we propose a hypothesis transfer strategy that leverages unlabeled target data to generate hypotheses for unlabeled source data, thereby enabling the pre-trained model to adapt to the target domain. Furthermore, we develop a semi-supervised domain adaptation method that utilizes these hypotheses to label source data, subsequently transferring the model to the target domain. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both image classification and semantic segmentation tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-00/S2DA.

Keywords: Source-free domain adaptation, hypothesis transfer, semi-supervised learning.

This study introduces a domain-informed neural network designed to identify charged particle interactions in astroparticle experiments. The method incorporates prior knowledge regarding the physics of particle interactions and their resulting signals, specifically utilizing the conservation of energy and momentum. By integrating these physical constraints, the model enhances the accuracy of interaction point reconstruction. We evaluated the approach using a Monte Carlo simulation of a Time Projection Chamber, comparing it against a standard Convolutional Neural Network that relies solely on spatial information. The results demonstrate that the domain-informed model outperforms the baseline, achieving a 10% improvement in the average 3D localization error. Furthermore, the model exhibits greater robustness to variations in input data quality and demonstrates superior performance in identifying interactions involving multiple particles. These findings indicate that domain-informed neural networks hold significant promise for advancing signal analysis in astroparticle physics. Atmospheric transmission spectroscopy serves as a vital instrument for characterizing the environments of exoplanets and brown dwarfs. This study introduces EXOPLINES, a database of molecular absorption cross-sections designed for the 0.6–5.0 $\mu$m wavelength range, covering 12 key species: H$_2$, H$_2$O, CH$_4$, NH$_3$, CO, CO$_2$, HCN, CS, H$_2$S, TiO, VO, and Na. EXOPLINES is built upon HITRAN 2016 data for H$_2$O, CH$_4$, NH$_3$, CO, CO$_2$, HCN, CS, H$_2$S, TiO, VO, and Na, alongside HITRAN 2022 data for H$_2$. The HITRAN 2022 release includes a new spectral line list for H$_2$ that extends the database's wavelength coverage to 0.6 $\mu$m. Additionally, we present a novel cross-section calculation for TiO, which was previously unavailable in HITRAN. We validate EXOPLINES by comparing synthetic spectra generated from the database against those produced by the ExoTransmit code. Furthermore, we apply EXOPLINES to model the transmission spectra of the exoplanets WASP-121b and WASP-18b, as well as the brown dwarfs 2MASS J0523-3627 and 2MASS J0523-3627. These models are compared against existing observations to evaluate the database's accuracy. EXOPLINES is accessible via the ExoMol website at http://www.exomol.com. This resource is intended to facilitate the modeling of atmospheric transmission spectra for brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets, thereby aiding in the interpretation of observational data. EXOPLINES is also integrated into the ExoMol Python package, available at https://github.com/exomol/exomol-python. We encourage the community to utilize EXOPLINES to advance the understanding of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres. This work establishes the first law for general quantum resource theories, extending the findings of [J. Eisert and M. Gellert, Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 200601 (2020)] from thermodynamics to broader resource frameworks. We demonstrate that any protocol converting a resource state $\rho$ into $\sigma$ while exchanging resourceless work $W$ adheres to the inequality $\Omega(\rho)-\Omega(\sigma)\leq W$, where $\Omega$ denotes a resource monotone. Furthermore, we prove that this first law remains valid even when accounting for losses, provided the loss is modeled as a quantum channel. Finally, we illustrate the application of these results within the context of coherence resource theories. These findings are anticipated to facilitate the analysis of resource transformations across diverse quantum resource theories. Additionally, we introduce a new class of quantum resource theories grounded in the concept of quantum channels possessing specific properties. This approach offers a unified framework for investigating various quantum resources and their associated conservation laws. We expect this new class to be applicable to a wide range of quantum resource theories. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the fundamental concepts of quantum resource theories; Section 3 presents our primary findings; Section 4 applies these results to coherence resource theories; and Section 5 concludes the study. Appendix A provides a proof of the first law for thermodynamics, while Appendix B details the construction of quantum resource theories based on channels with particular characteristics. Appendix C demonstrates that the first law for coherence resource theories can be derived from the first law for general quantum resource theories. Finally, Appendix D explores the relationship between the first law and the second law of quantum resource theories. We introduce a family of good quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes capable of being decoded in linear time. Specifically, for a block length of $n$, the rate is $\Omega(n^{-1/2})$ and the decoding complexity is $O(n)$. Our construction utilizes a concatenation of two specific qLDPC codes: the hypergraph product (HP) code and the surface code. The HP code features a rate of $\Theta(n^{-1/2})$ and a distance of $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$, while the surface code has a rate of $\Theta(1)$ and a distance of $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. By concatenating these codes, we achieve a distance of $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ and a rate of $\Theta(n^{-1/2})$. We demonstrate that the resulting code maintains linear-time decoding complexity, even when accounting for the overhead introduced by concatenation. Furthermore, we establish that the HP code can be decoded in linear time even under a constant fraction of errors, provided the error distribution is uniform. This result relies on a novel, general technique for bounding the runtime of a Markov chain, which we believe will be applicable to other decoding problems. Our findings represent the first instance of a good qLDPC code with linear-time decoding complexity, improving upon the previous best complexity of $O(n^{3/2})$. Additionally, our work provides the first non-trivial upper bound on the runtime of a Markov chain defined by a sparse graph, a problem that has remained unresolved for over a decade. Finally, we show that our construction can be extended to concatenated qLDPC codes with constant rate and linear-time decoding complexity. This is achieved by concatenating the HP code with a family of good, constant-rate, constant-time qLDPC codes recently developed by Hastings and Roth. This result marks the first demonstration that good qLDPC codes can be decoded in constant time. Our work also offers the first non-trivial upper bound on the runtime of a Markov chain defined by a sparse graph with constant rate and constant distance. We demonstrate that for graphs with a girth exceeding $4r+1$, the distributed distance-$r$ domination number is bounded below by $\Omega(n/\Delta)$, where $n$ represents the node count and $\Delta$ denotes the maximum degree. This finding indicates that distributed algorithms cannot achieve a dominating set size smaller than $\Omega(n/\Delta)$ in high-girth graphs. Furthermore, we present a randomized distributed algorithm capable of generating a distance-$r$ dominating set of size $O(n/\Delta)$ with high probability. Additionally, we explore the distributed identification of graphs that lack a distance-$r$ dominating set of size $O(n/\Delta)$. Our results establish that identifying such graphs requires at least $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ rounds, a lower bound that is tight up to constant factors. This is achieved through a randomized distributed algorithm that identifies these graphs in $O(\sqrt{n})$ rounds with high probability. Finally, we extend our findings to the context of dominating sets in low-girth graphs. This study examines the bulk-boundary correspondence in disordered higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs) by analyzing the emergence of boundary states. We demonstrate that the bulk-boundary correspondence for boundary states in HOTIs is governed by the bulk-boundary correspondence of the bulk state. Furthermore, we show that the bulk-boundary correspondence for hinge states is disrupted by disorder, whereas the bulk-boundary correspondence for edge states remains robust against disorder. These findings are illustrated through the specific example of the disordered Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang model. Our results provide a theoretical basis for the stability of boundary states in disordered HOTIs. Additionally, we discuss the bulk-boundary correspondence within the framework of the topological field theory of HOTIs. Finally, we explore the bulk-boundary correspondence in the context of the topological classification of HOTIs. The dataset comprises 1,000 observations of 100 targets, with a median of 12 speckle frames per target. The analysis successfully resolved 1,100 binary systems, of which 60% were previously unresolved. The study reports a binary detection rate of 11% and a binary fraction of 22% for the sample. A catalog of 1,100 resolved binaries is provided, featuring separation measurements with a median precision of 0.001 arcsec. The catalog also includes measurements for 1,000 single stars, with a median photometric accuracy of 0.001 mag. This work represents the most recent speckle interferometry results from SOAR. This study presents the first multi-frequency LOFAR observations of a jet-driven piston shock within the low solar corona. The jet's morphology and dynamics were also examined, showing a narrow, well-collimated structure with a speed of approximately 1000 km/s. We introduce a new random vortex dynamics model for the Euler equations, formulated as a functional stochastic differential equation (F-SDE) that evolves both vortices and their interactions. This F-SDE is derived from a novel variational principle involving a stochastic Hamiltonian, which extends the deterministic Hamiltonian of point vortex systems. We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for this equation and demonstrate that it preserves key physical invariants, including energy, momentum, and Casimirs. Furthermore, we prove that the system's solutions converge to the Euler equation's solution as noise intensity approaches zero. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to illustrate the model's performance. These results indicate that the proposed method effectively captures the large-scale behavior of two-dimensional incompressible Euler flows, offering a promising framework for simulating two-dimensional turbulence. Additionally, the method is shown to be computationally efficient, with a complexity comparable to that of the vorticity confinement method. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's advantages and potential applications. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to be efficiently executed on quantum hardware but difficult to simulate classically. While the output probability distributions of the quantum states are classically intractable to calculate, the individual output states themselves can be determined. This work investigates the entanglement within the complete state vector of boson sampling, revealing that it scales exponentially with the number of output modes. Furthermore, we establish that the entanglement of the quantum state associated with $N$ input modes across $M$ output modes is bounded by $\min(N, M)$. These findings are derived through the application of the Schmidt decomposition and the permanent's semipositive-definite property. Additionally, we demonstrate that the entanglement of a single output mode with the remainder of the system is bounded by 1. Finally, we examine the entanglement of the quantum state corresponding to a specific input configuration in the dual-rail encoding of boson sampling. By utilizing the properties of the permanent and the von Neumann entropy, we prove that the entanglement between any two dual-rail modes is bounded by 1. These results offer valuable insights into the entanglement structure of boson sampling, which is essential for developing quantum error correction methods. Temporal data analysis is essential for comprehending the dynamics of biological systems. However, temporal sequences in life sciences often consist of few data points, possess high dimensionality, and are typically recorded over extended periods. This study introduces a supervised learning approach utilizing a recurrent neural network to forecast the subsequent time point within a sequence. We demonstrate that this method surpasses other machine learning techniques in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we apply this learning framework to identify the temporal relationships between gene expression levels in *C. elegans* and *Drosophila*. Our findings reveal that the model successfully captures the temporal interactions between genes, with the resulting network topology aligning closely with established biological knowledge. These results indicate that our approach effectively extracts temporal information from short, high-dimensional sequences, thereby offering a robust tool for analyzing temporal data in life sciences. Reinforcement learning (RL) focuses on agents interacting with environments to maximize long-term rewards. However, many real-world scenarios involve partial observability, where agents cannot access complete information. This paper examines how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) function within such settings. We demonstrate that RNNs can be interpreted as belief state machines, where the hidden state represents a belief state—a probability distribution over the true underlying state. This interpretation holds for any RNN, regardless of its architecture, provided the transition and observation models are linear. Furthermore, we establish that the KL divergence between two belief states generated by RNNs is bounded by the sum of the KL divergences of their transition models. Finally, we apply these findings to analyze the behavior of various RL algorithms utilizing RNNs. Our results indicate that these algorithms may fail to converge to optimal policies when the transition model is inaccurate, a common issue in partially observable environments. Additionally, we show that these methods can converge to sub-optimal policies even when the transition model is accurate. These insights are validated through experiments on a grid-world task. This paper introduces Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to enhance the accuracy of table extraction from such documents. We introduce a multi-stage game of incomplete information featuring multiple players, where each participant possesses a belief system regarding the others' types and strategies. We demonstrate that a cognitive hierarchy equilibrium exists for this game, characterized by a finite hierarchy of beliefs. Furthermore, we establish that cognitive hierarchy equilibria converge to Nash equilibria as the hierarchy level approaches infinity. Finally, we examine the relationship between cognitive hierarchy equilibria and quantal response equilibrium. In the context of a two-player, two-action stage game, we prove that when the payoff matrix is symmetric, the cognitive hierarchy limit coincides with the quantal response equilibrium limit. Additionally, we provide a counterexample showing this equivalence does not hold in the general case. This paper extends the findings of [1] to the domain of multi-stage games of incomplete information.

Accurate population estimates are essential for effective resource allocation and the formulation of public policies. This study introduces a novel approach to population estimation that integrates geospatial data with historical census records. By utilizing a geostatistical model, the research analyzes the spatial distribution of populations across administrative units in Mozambique. The methodology employs a geographically weighted regression model to derive a population density surface, which is subsequently smoothed using a kriging model to generate a continuous population estimate for the country. The findings indicate that this technique offers a dependable and sustainable means of estimating population figures. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the proposed method can be effectively applied to other nations possessing accessible geospatial and census data. Approximate membership query (AMQ) filters are space-efficient data structures designed to determine whether elements likely belong to a set. While these filters inherently allow for false positives, we introduce a novel AMQ filter capable of identifying all elements that do not exist in the set with absolute certainty. This structure maintains the standard space and query time complexities of conventional AMQ filters. We provide a theoretical analysis of our approach and validate its performance through experimental results. Our findings demonstrate that this new filter outperforms existing AMQ filters in terms of both space utilization and query speed. Furthermore, we highlight its significant potential for enhancing the efficiency of various applications, including the parallelization of AMQ filters and the construction of inverted indexes. We present a theoretical framework for converting atoms into molecules through laser-induced three-body recombination. This approach offers an alternative to current methods for creating ultracold molecules, which typically rely on photoassociation. In this scheme, the binding energy of the resulting molecule is absorbed by a third atom, while a laser facilitates the reaction by enabling the spin flip of one atom. We demonstrate that this process can achieve a conversion efficiency of approximately 10% and produce a molecular flux of about $10^4$ molecules per second. Furthermore, we explore the potential for further enhancing conversion rates by utilizing multiple molecular states. This technique is applicable to atoms and molecules within the same hyperfine spin manifold, such as $^{6}$Li or $^{40}$K. Additionally, we examine the potential for generating ultracold molecules in vibrational excited states. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of this method for studying few-body physics. Pitch control is a fundamental aspect of speech synthesis, yet it is difficult to achieve while maintaining naturalness and timbre. The recently introduced neural TTS system, FastPitch, utilizes a pitch contour as an input to enhance controllability; however, this method often results in degraded speech quality and a loss of timbre. To address this, we introduce a timbre-preserving pitch augmentation technique that generates multiple pitch contours with varying fundamental frequencies (F0) while keeping the pitch contour (PC) intact. This approach is integrated into FastPitch to boost timbre preservation during pitch shifting. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves the pitch controllability of FastPitch. Additionally, we present a pitch-shifting application built upon this method, which allows users to adjust the F0 of speech without compromising its timbre. This study investigates the production of lepton pairs alongside $b\bar{b}$ pairs at the LHC, with a specific focus on the impact of $b$-quark fragmentation on the precision of the $W$ boson mass measurement. Using the POWHEG-BOX and PYTHIA 8 event generators, we simulate the process $pp\to W(\to \ell\nu) + b\bar{b}$ at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. We examine how various experimental observables, derived from the invariant mass distribution of the lepton and the $b$-jets, are influenced by $b$-quark fragmentation. Our analysis demonstrates that the $W$ boson mass can be determined with a precision of approximately 10 MeV, provided that the effects of $b$-quark fragmentation are accurately modeled. Furthermore, we show that this high precision is achievable even when relying solely on the invariant mass of the $b$-jets. These findings are crucial for the upcoming ATLAS and CMS measurements of the $W$ boson mass. Additionally, we explore the potential of this method for future high-precision determinations of the $W$ boson mass at the High-Luminosity LHC. We examine how the accretion of a binary affects the final masses of the planets and the disk's structural evolution. This approach utilizes the entropy of each feature to calculate its corresponding weight, ensuring that features with higher entropy receive lower weights. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of clustering quality. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become a cornerstone of deep learning, offering a flexible architecture that combines multiple expert networks to handle complex tasks. Despite their widespread adoption, the theoretical foundations of learning MoE remain underdeveloped. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a consistent and computationally efficient algorithm for learning MoE under the realizable setting. Our approach utilizes a novel change-of-variable technique to transform the original non-convex problem into a convex one, enabling the application of established convex optimization methods. We demonstrate that our algorithm achieves a sample complexity of $O(d^2/\epsilon^2)$, where $d$ represents the number of experts and $\epsilon$ denotes the target accuracy. Furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound of $\Omega(d^2/\epsilon^2)$, proving that our upper bound is optimal. These findings offer a comprehensive theoretical understanding of MoE learning and highlight the potential for advancing both the theory and practice of mixture models. Specifically, we establish that the breaking of any global symmetry in a quantum gravity framework must occur at an energy scale exceeding $10^{11}$ GeV, a threshold derived from CMB observations. This constraint is independent of the specific quantum gravity model, provided the breaking of global symmetries is not driven by a CMB birefringence mechanism. Furthermore, we show that this limit can be strengthened to $10^{12}$ GeV if the cosmic birefringence angle is determined to be non-zero. These findings are particularly pertinent to the breaking of the electroweak global $SU(2)_L$ symmetry in quantum gravity, a scenario that could account for the observed CMB birefringence. Additionally, we highlight that this lower bound on the breaking energy scale is significantly lower than the $10^{16}$ GeV limit inferred from the non-observation of proton decay. Finally, we note that this lower bound is expected to improve as CMB birefringence measurements become more precise. The transferability of deep neural networks (DNNs) is a critical factor influencing their deployment in real-world applications. This paper re-examines two prevailing consensuses regarding transferability: (1) the belief that transferability is inherent to deep architectures, and (2) the notion that pre-training on large-scale datasets is essential for achieving transferability. To address these issues, we introduce a new training framework designed to enhance transferability by integrating a novel data augmentation strategy with a specialized loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in both transferability and generalization. Furthermore, our method successfully improves the performance of DNNs trained from scratch, thereby challenging the first consensus. Additionally, our findings indicate that pre-training on large-scale datasets is not a prerequisite for transferability, contradicting the second consensus. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our method across various application scenarios, including semi-supervised learning, domain adaptation, and multi-task learning. The spread of information within social networks is a critical factor influencing the adoption of new products and services. This study investigates how a network's modular structure impacts the velocity of information diffusion. We introduce a model where a network is divided into modules, and information spreads from a randomly selected node within a chosen module to other nodes in that same module. Our findings indicate that the diffusion speed is governed by the network's modular architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the relationship between modularity and diffusion speed is non-monotonic, meaning that increasing modularity does not consistently accelerate information spread. These results are validated through simulations on both real-world and synthetic networks. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for designing social networks to facilitate the rapid dissemination of information. This study introduces an accuracy analysis for the time-domain regular perturbation model applied to unamplified links in discrete-time nonlinear Schrödinger equations. The analysis demonstrates that the model yields exact results for the first-order perturbation and provides exact expressions for the first three coefficients of the first-order perturbation expansion within the error term. Leveraging these findings, the paper establishes the convergence of the perturbation series for the mean squared error of a single channel in a lumped fiber link. Furthermore, it proves that the model achieves an accuracy of $O(\epsilon^2)$ for the mean power of a single channel in a lumped fiber link, where $\epsilon$ denotes the small parameter in the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to validate the theoretical results. The discussion highlights that this model is highly accurate for unamplified links, even when accounting for higher-order effects. Consequently, the proposed model and its associated theoretical analysis offer a valuable tool for analyzing and designing optical communication systems that utilize lumped amplification. Additionally, the methodology can be extended to analyze the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with distributed Raman amplification. The paper concludes by outlining several potential directions for future research. We present a reentrant quantum Hall phase characterized by a filling factor of 5/2, which emerges at moderate levels of Landau-level mixing. This phase is identified through the reappearance of a distinct plateau in the Hall conductivity. Our findings indicate that this reentrant phase is intrinsically linked to the reentrant 3/2 quantum Hall phase. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reentrant 5/2 phase exhibits a dependence on both the disorder strength and the ratio of Zeeman splitting to Landau-level mixing. These results offer valuable insights into the nature of the 5/2 quantum Hall state. Additionally, we explore the potential for observing this reentrant phase in experimental settings. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results regarding the topological nature of the 5/2 quantum Hall phase. The recent discovery of gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers has sparked significant interest in primordial black holes (PBHs) as a potential dark matter candidate. This study examines the cosmological evolution of PBHs, specifically addressing the impact of the Thakurta metric on their dynamics. We demonstrate that PBHs within the cosmological environment are not accurately described by the Thakurta metric. Consequently, our findings indicate that the existing LIGO-Virgo constraints on PBHs are unaffected by this metric. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these results for PBHs as dark matter candidates. Finally, we analyze the cosmological evolution of PBHs across various mass scales, revealing that they can influence the formation of large-scale structures. This effect is particularly pronounced for intermediate-mass PBHs, which can significantly alter the evolution of the universe. These conclusions are supported by numerical simulations. Our results suggest that PBHs with masses between $10^{10}$ and $10^{12}$ solar masses could account for a substantial portion of dark matter. Additionally, we note that the Thakurta metric may have implications for the accretion of matter by supermassive black holes. Pebble accretion is a leading theory for planet formation, positing that protoplanets grow by capturing pebbles drifting inward from the outer disk. This process is highly sensitive to the local dust density, which is determined by the gas-to-dust ratio. In this study, we examine how dust density perturbations, generated by the streaming instability, influence pebble accretion and the resulting planet mass distribution. We employ a 1D model to simulate the evolution of dust density and planet mass, incorporating a feedback mechanism where planetesimals form in high-dust regions and subsequently deplete them. Our results indicate that this feedback loop can produce a power-law distribution of planet masses with a slope of approximately -1.5, closely matching the observed distribution of giant planets. Furthermore, we find that the planet mass distribution is significantly affected by the initial dust-to-gas ratio, with higher initial dust concentrations yielding fewer massive planets. These findings suggest that the streaming instability and pebble accretion can naturally account for the observed characteristics of giant planets. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for the formation of super-Jupiter planets. Finally, we discuss the potential impact of dust density perturbations on the formation of terrestrial planets. Our findings suggest that the streaming instability can generate a clumpy disk structure, which may explain the observed variations in dust density within the inner disk. This variability could influence the formation of terrestrial planets, potentially explaining the diverse compositions of terrestrial planets found in different systems. Overall, our results highlight the critical role of dust density perturbations in planet formation and suggest that future observations should focus on detecting these perturbations in protoplanetary disks. This will provide valuable insights into the planet formation process and help us better understand the origins of planetary systems. Overparameterized models, characterized by a parameter count exceeding the number of training samples, are a standard feature of modern machine learning. This paper investigates the origins of this phenomenon, demonstrating that computational limitations in learning algorithms can necessitate overparameterization. Specifically, we examine the gradient descent algorithm applied to linear regression, where the objective is to minimize the squared error. We establish that for any sample size $n$, there exist specific datasets requiring at least $\Omega(n^2)$ parameters to learn within a reasonable timeframe. Furthermore, we prove that for certain datasets, the sample complexity of gradient descent scales with the required parameter count, meaning that increasing the parameter budget directly increases the number of samples needed for successful learning. Finally, we extend these findings to support vector machines, indicating that similar constraints apply to this model as well. Collectively, these results highlight that the prevalence of overparameterization in contemporary machine learning may stem from the computational characteristics of the algorithms employed. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the parameter count and the generalization capabilities of gradient descent in linear regression. Our analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, the generalization error of gradient descent scales with the parameter count, suggesting that overparameterization can lead to poor generalization. This insight underscores the critical importance of selecting appropriate algorithms when utilizing overparameterized models. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents our main findings; Section 3 provides the proofs for these results; and Section 4 offers a discussion of related work. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines potential directions for future research. This paper establishes a relative version of the Balog-Szemer\'edi-Gowers theorem within countable abelian groups. Specifically, given a set $A$ in a group $G$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, if the product $|A||A-A|$ is less than $|G|$ and $A$ contains a subset $X$ of size $|G|^\varepsilon$ such that the sum $X+X$ possesses small doubling relative to $|G|$, then $A$ contains a Bohr set of size $|G|^\varepsilon$. This finding serves as the foundational tool for proving a relative analogue of the Balog-Szemer\'edi-Gowers theorem in the same context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this result is optimal by constructing a family of examples in the group $\mathbb{Z}_2 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathbb{Z}_2$ where the Bohr set size cannot be improved. These examples also illustrate the necessity of the small doubling condition on $X+X$. Finally, we provide an alternative proof of the original Balog-Szemer\'edi-Gowers theorem in abelian groups, which relies on the same techniques used to prove the main result. This study addresses an urban dial-a-ride problem featuring flexible time windows, a heterogeneous fleet, and a limit on the number of passengers. We introduce a Branch-and-Cut algorithm that utilizes a mixed-integer programming formulation enhanced with various valid inequalities. Furthermore, we propose a heuristic designed to generate high-quality feasible solutions. Finally, computational experiments are conducted to evaluate the performance of both the heuristic and the exact algorithm. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively solves small and medium-sized instances. Additionally, the heuristic consistently produces high-quality solutions for larger instances, achieving an average gap of 1.1% relative to the lower bounds provided by the exact algorithm. A key advantage of this method is its ability to determine the optimality of the solutions found by the heuristic. The paper concludes with a discussion on potential avenues for future research. We introduce a model describing a strongly correlated metal with spin-orbit coupling, where the latter is significantly amplified by strong Coulomb repulsion. This mechanism is demonstrated in the three-band Hubbard model, which captures the essential physics of the $d$-electron system in iridates. The model's validity is confirmed by comparing its predictions with those of the three-band model for $5d^2$ Ruddlesden-Popper oxides. Furthermore, we derive the quasiparticle spectrum and discuss the resulting implications. This mechanism is expected to be prevalent in materials featuring narrow bands and strong Coulomb repulsion, including iridates, ruthenates, and nickelates. Additionally, it may play a crucial role in the physics of twisted bilayer graphene. Finally, we highlight the potential for this approach to enable the design of novel correlated materials. We introduce a novel dark matter candidate termed metastable conformal dark matter (MeCoDM). This model features a fermionic dark matter particle that remains stable due to an approximate conformal symmetry, which is spontaneously broken by the dark matter itself. Consequently, the fermion acquires a mass that scales with the vacuum expectation value of the associated fermion bilinear. This mass is sufficiently small to ensure the particle's abundance matches observational limits, yet large enough to prevent significant scattering off nucleons. Furthermore, the model offers a natural explanation for the observed dark matter density. Finally, we examine the implications of this framework for direct detection experiments and discuss its potential to resolve the Hubble tension. Additionally, we explore the possibility that MeCoDM could account for the recently reported $1.3\,\mathrm{GeV}$ excess in the electron recoil spectrum from the XENON1T experiment. In this scenario, the dark matter would possess a mass of approximately $1.3\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and a decay width of roughly $10^{-19}\,\mathrm{eV}$. Such a particle could be produced via the decay of a light scalar particle, which itself might arise from the decay of a heavier particle. This mechanism could also contribute to alleviating the Hubble tension. Finally, we demonstrate that MeCoDM can explain the anomalous dark matter signal detected by the DAMA/LIBRA experiment. In this case, the dark matter mass is approximately $10\,\mathrm{GeV}$, and its decay width is around $10^{-21}\,\mathrm{eV}$. The DAMA/LIBRA signal can be reproduced if the dark matter decays into a neutrino and a dark photon, with the dark photon subsequently decaying into an electron-positron pair. This scenario is viable if the dark photon mass is below $10\,\mathrm{MeV}$ and its coupling to electrons is approximately $10^{-10}$. Such a dark photon could be generated through the decay of a light scalar, which in turn decays from a heavier particle. This production mechanism also offers a potential resolution to the Hubble tension. Finally, we show that MeCoDM can also account for the recent XENON1T excess. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly being deployed in clinical settings, yet their performance often degrades when real-world data distributions differ from training distributions. This study introduces a framework for assessing the test performance of AI medical devices undergoing distribution shifts. The approach integrates a data-driven method for estimating distribution shifts with conformal prediction, a technique for generating valid statistical prediction intervals. Furthermore, we show that the method can identify the specific covariates driving the shift, offering a pathway to enhance the robustness of AI medical devices. These findings hold significant implications for the clinical adoption of AI medical devices, as they enable clinicians to make more informed decisions regarding their use. Additionally, the method can be extended to other clinical AI applications, such as those involving chest X-rays or brain MRI scans. The arithmetic coding method known as the Numerical Representation of Information (ANS) is renowned for its high compression efficiency, which has made it a standard in modern compression formats. This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the ANS algorithm's performance. We demonstrate that the ANS encoder operates with a time complexity of $O(\log n)$, where $n$ represents the length of the input bitstream. Furthermore, we establish that the ANS-compressed bitstream achieves an entropy rate of $H(p) + O(1/n)$, where $H(p)$ denotes the entropy rate of the source. These findings indicate that ANS compression is asymptotically optimal. Additionally, we prove that the ANS decoder is deterministic. Our approach relies on a novel theoretical framework for the ANS algorithm, which we term the "ANS tree." This paper also provides a rigorous proof of the equivalence between the ANS tree and the original ANS algorithm. The ANS tree offers a more intuitive and mathematically tractable representation of the algorithm, facilitating the proofs of its properties. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of the ANS tree's characteristics. Finally, we extend the ANS algorithm to handle non-uniform symbol distributions and prove that this generalized version maintains asymptotic optimality. The ANS tree is also applicable to other entropy encoding methods, such as range encoding. We illustrate this by applying the ANS tree to range encoding and proving its optimality. The ANS tree provides a unified theoretical foundation for analyzing the efficiency of various entropy encoding algorithms. The dielectric characteristics of cement-based materials are primarily determined by the properties of their pore solutions. This study investigates the frequency-dependent dielectric behavior of these solutions across a broad spectrum of cement compositions and water-to-binder ratios. By combining experimental data with a theoretical model, we establish a comprehensive understanding of the dielectric response in cement-based systems. This understanding is essential for interpreting the dielectric properties of the final material and for developing new methods to monitor the hydration process. Specifically, we demonstrate that the dielectric response of cement-based materials can be separated into two distinct components: one attributed to the solid cement matrix and another to the pore solution. Furthermore, we show that the dielectric response of the pore solution is independent of the specific cement type and water-to-binder ratio, relying solely on the solution's ionic concentration. Finally, we provide a quantitative analysis of the dielectric response as a function of ionic concentration. These findings are derived from measurements of the dielectric permittivity and conductivity of various cement-based materials. The results indicate that the dielectric response of the solid matrix remains constant across different water-to-binder ratios and cement types, whereas the response of the pore solution is governed exclusively by the ionic concentration. Additionally, we observe that the dielectric response of the solid matrix is independent of the ionic concentration of the pore solution. These conclusions are supported by a theoretical framework that incorporates the dielectric properties of both the solid matrix and the pore solution. This model enables the prediction of the dielectric response for any cement-based material, provided the ionic concentration of the pore solution is known. The proposed approach offers a robust method for characterizing cement-based materials and holds significant potential for monitoring the hydration process. Ultimately, this work provides a solid foundation for the development of dielectric sensors designed to measure ionic concentration in cement-based systems. Such sensors could be integrated into cement-based structures to facilitate real-time monitoring of the material's performance. This study examines the driving forces behind the development of military drone swarms by analyzing scientific literature on the topic. We employ a data-driven natural language processing (NLP) approach to extract key terms from the texts, which are subsequently visualized using a network graph. This graph illustrates the relationships between these terms, allowing researchers to identify the primary drivers of swarm drone technology. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that concepts such as "communication," "control," and "autonomy" are also fundamental to the field. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential of NLP methods to efficiently extract critical information from large volumes of data, offering a valuable tool for analyzing extensive scientific corpora. We introduce a direct cosmological inference method utilizing three-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ forest correlations, which simultaneously determines the Hubble parameter ($H_0$) and the matter density parameter ($\Omega_m$). This approach relies on the fact that the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest's three-point correlation function is sensitive to the comoving volume, thereby encoding information about the expansion rate and matter density. By employing a machine learning model to generate synthetic Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data, we demonstrate that this method can directly infer $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$ with a precision of approximately 10% using a single redshift bin. Furthermore, we show that combining multiple redshift bins enhances the accuracy of these inferences. Our results indicate that this technique offers a complementary perspective to other cosmological probes, such as the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest power spectrum and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations. Additionally, we highlight that the method's accuracy is significantly influenced by the quality of the synthetic data, underscoring the necessity for high-fidelity simulations. This study represents the initial exploration of the three-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ forest correlation as a cosmological probe, with future investigations expected to yield more precise outcomes. Predicting trajectories for autonomous driving is a critical challenge. While Conditional Variational Autoencoders (CVAEs) are widely used, they often fail to account for social interactions, leading to inaccurate predictions. To address this, we introduce a novel framework called Sliding Sequential CVAE with Time Variant Socially-aware Rethinking (SSCVAE). This approach employs a recurrent network to generate a sequence of CVAEs, where each CVAE predicts a trajectory segment conditioned on the previous one. Furthermore, we incorporate a socially-aware rethinking module that adjusts the predicted trajectory based on the current state of surrounding vehicles. Experimental results demonstrate that SSCVAE outperforms existing methods in predicting trajectories for autonomous driving scenarios. This study examines the relationships among three information-theoretic metrics for complex systems: the mutual information between a system's state and its parameters, the mutual information between two distinct states given the parameters, and the mutual information between the parameters and a target output. We demonstrate that these measures are not equivalent and explore the implications of this finding for defining complexity in artificial neural networks. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of these measures across various network architectures, including the Hopfield model, Boltzmann machines, and autoencoders. Our results indicate that while these measures align in simpler systems, they diverge in more complex configurations, such as Boltzmann machines. Finally, we illustrate how these information-theoretic tools can be employed to investigate the internal representations of trained neural networks. This study introduces a new framework designed to facilitate interaction between humans and swarms of robots. The system utilizes a deep neural network to identify a sequence of hand gestures, enabling users to control robot movements and formations through natural hand signals. By leveraging the inherent parallelism of the network architecture, the proposed method achieves real-time gesture recognition. Furthermore, the system is engineered to operate in a decentralized fashion, allowing for scalability across varying numbers of robots and users. The efficacy of this approach is validated through a proof-of-concept implementation featuring a deep neural network and a robotic swarm. The results demonstrate that the system can reliably recognize gesture sequences with high accuracy while maintaining real-time performance. Additionally, the system exhibits robustness against occlusions and minor variations in gesture execution. These findings indicate that the proposed system is well-suited for practical applications in both indoor and outdoor environments. Counterdiabatic driving (CD) is a method designed to accelerate adiabatic evolution by eliminating non-adiabatic transitions. While CD has been extensively applied to quantum annealing and adiabatic quantum computing, its potential for quantum simulation remains underexplored. This study demonstrates that CD can significantly enhance the performance of variational algorithms for preparing the ground state of the Hubbard model. By applying CD to the variational adiabatic algorithm, we achieve a substantial reduction in the number of required iterations. Furthermore, we show that this approach enables the preparation of the Hubbard model's ground state across a broader parameter range. These findings indicate that CD is a valuable tool for advancing quantum simulation techniques. Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of implementing this CD-optimized variational algorithm on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. Our results suggest that such devices could simulate the Hubbard model in two dimensions with up to 16 sites. Finally, we outline potential applications of this algorithm in quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics. The accompanying Python code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/CD-optimized-variational-algorithm. We demonstrate that any harmonic map from a compact Riemann surface to a CAT($k$) sphere, which is not constant, constitutes a topological covering. This finding extends a result by Schoen and Yau regarding minimal surfaces and aligns with the findings of Schoen and Yau concerning harmonic maps into hyperbolic spaces. Furthermore, we establish that any uniformization of a compact surface into a CAT($k$) sphere can be realized as a harmonic map, thereby generalizing the classical uniformization theorem. Additionally, we prove that any harmonic map from a compact Riemann surface to a CAT($k$) sphere that is not a topological covering must be constant. These results are derived from a more general theorem concerning the stability of harmonic maps between compact manifolds with non-positive curvature. Finally, we present an application of this theorem to the study of harmonic maps between compact manifolds with non-negative curvature. In this context, we show that if a harmonic map is not a topological covering, it is homotopic to a constant map, provided the source manifold possesses a non-trivial first homology group. This finding generalizes the work of Schoen and Yau on minimal surfaces and is consistent with the results of Schoen and Yau regarding minimal surfaces in positively curved manifolds. The paper also includes a discussion of the broader implications of these findings. The primary tool employed is the Bochner technique, which has been utilized in various contexts, including the work of Schoen and Yau. The techniques developed herein may have applications in other areas of differential geometry. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. We introduce a laser-plasma system designed to generate intense, ultrashort photon-photon interactions. This platform utilizes a laser-driven electron beam to create a photon-photon collider, where the electron beam is directed into a gas jet to produce high-energy photons. These photons subsequently interact within a plasma medium. We demonstrate that this setup can achieve photon-photon scattering cross-sections exceeding $10^{-24}$ cm$^2$, surpassing the capabilities of current and upcoming collider facilities. Furthermore, we outline the necessary laser and plasma parameters to realize this system. Our proposed collider could enable the study of photon-photon scattering and the search for light-by-light interactions mediated by heavy charged particles, such as the $W$ boson. Additionally, this platform offers a means to investigate the non-linear quantum electrodynamics vacuum, including phenomena like vacuum birefringence and photon splitting. We also discuss the potential for photon-photon interactions occurring within the laser acceleration stage itself. This proposal represents a significant step toward a photon-photon collider, which could serve as a complementary tool to traditional colliders for exploring new physics. Such a device would facilitate investigations into the quantum nature of light and the search for physics beyond the Standard Model. The proposed collider could be implemented in the near future using existing laser and plasma technology. We anticipate that this system will open a new field of research focused on photon-photon physics. This work was conducted under the European Research Council (ERC) Advanced Grant 320547 (QPLASMA). Data exchange problems involve mapping a source structure to a target structure under specific constraints. This paper examines data exchange from relational databases to RDF graphs, focusing on cases where the target RDF schema is defined by shape expressions. We investigate the existence of universal relations and the existence and size of quasi universal relations. Our findings indicate that universal relations exist precisely when the size of quasi universal relations remains constant relative to the source database. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this constant size is linear if and only if the shape expression schema adheres to a specific structural condition. Finally, we establish that these structural conditions are decidable. The paper also includes illustrative examples. This study examines the production of top quark pairs accompanied by a new light scalar particle, $\phi$, at the LHC. The analysis focuses on scenarios where the scalar decays into a pair of soft photons, a channel that remains largely unexplored. We establish exclusion limits on the coupling between top quarks and the scalar, assuming a mass of $\phi$ at 10 GeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these constraints can be significantly strengthened by incorporating data from future LHC runs. Finally, we explore the potential of the LHC to detect such a light scalar within the framework of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM). In this context, the light scalar is identified as the CP-even Higgs boson, and we show that its existence is permitted by the derived limits. Additionally, we investigate how the constraints on the top-scalar coupling can be translated into limits on the MSSM parameter space. This approach involves a one-to-one mapping of the top-scalar coupling to the ratio of vacuum expectation values, $\tan\beta$, and the mixing angle, $\alpha$, which is subsequently constrained by the LHC's Higgs boson search results. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the parameter space of the MSSM. The findings of this work are accessible at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.00001}. The accompanying Python code can be found at \url{https://github.com/Ankit-12345/TopPhiProduction}. The analysis was performed using the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and MadAnalysis5 software packages. We conducted a spectroscopic analysis of 11 Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus region, utilizing high-resolution spectra obtained with the UVES spectrograph on the VLT. Our findings indicate that these stars possess masses ranging from 10 to 15 solar masses and effective temperatures between 14,000 and 17,000 K. The Be stars HD 93126A and HD 93126B exhibit the highest projected rotational velocities ($v\sin i$) at 200 and 180 km/s, respectively, while HD 93126C and HD 93126D show the lowest values at 30 and 40 km/s. Furthermore, the Be stars HD 93126A, HD 93126B, and HD 93126C display emission lines in their spectra, suggesting they are in the early stages of Be star evolution. Conversely, HD 93126D, HD 93126E, and HD 93126F exhibit absorption lines, indicating they are in the late stages of evolution. Additionally, HD 93126D, HD 93126E, and HD 93126F are identified as binary systems. Finally, we determined the masses and masses-to-luminosities ratios for these stars, revealing that HD 93126A, HD 93126B, and HD 93126C have the highest mass-to-luminosity ratios, whereas HD 93126D, HD 93126E, and HD 93126F have the lowest. These results suggest that HD 93126A, HD 93126B, and HD 93126C are in the early evolutionary stages, while HD 93126D, HD 93126E, and HD 93126F are in the late stages. This study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the 30 Doradus region. (Abridged)

Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining multiple augmentation approaches produces the most substantial improvements. Finally, we explore the potential of these techniques to reduce reliance on synthetic data in future ITN systems. By leveraging the non-fungible characteristics of data points, we develop a new kernel known as the Non-Fungible Tangent Kernel (NFT-K). This approach enables the learning of tangent kernels using data that resides on a manifold. Our findings demonstrate that NFT-K kernels are non-negative, positive definite, and Lipschitz continuous. Furthermore, we establish that NFT-K kernels are Lipschitz equivalent to a specific family of positive definite kernels defined on the manifold. We also present a theoretical analysis of the generalization error for NFT-K kernels, proving that they converge to the true tangent kernel as the sample size increases. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of NFT-K kernels through experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets. These results indicate that NFT-K kernels outperform existing tangent kernel methods in terms of classification accuracy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/NFT-K. This study examines the integration of social speaker characteristics into synthetic speech. We begin by reviewing prior research on character voice synthesis, followed by an analysis of the challenges involved in embedding these traits. To address these issues, we propose a framework that combines neural text-to-speech models with controlled speech manipulation. This study examines the collective motion of nuclei using the generalized harmonic oscillator model, incorporating a minimal length via the deformed Heisenberg algebra. The resulting energy spectrum and wave functions are derived via the algebraic method, revealing that the minimal length significantly influences the energy levels of deformed nuclei. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the minimal length parameter can be determined from experimental data regarding energy levels. Finally, the analysis indicates that the minimal length effect is more pronounced in lighter nuclei compared to heavier ones. These findings are corroborated by comparing the calculated spectra with experimental data for various nuclei. Additionally, the calculated root mean square radius for the nucleus $^{168}$Er aligns well with experimental measurements. The research concludes that the minimal length concept offers a viable framework for analyzing collective motion in nuclei. Finally, the study explores the potential for further investigation into the minimal length effect within the context of nuclear physics. This paper introduces multiple new classes of polyphase Golay complementary arrays (PGCA) across various dimensions. Specifically, we present new binary and polyphase sequences that are Golay complementary (GC) of degree 2, alongside new PGCA constructions in dimensions 2, 3, and 4. Additionally, we provide new GC sequences of degree 4 and propose a general method for generating PGCA sequences of any dimension using existing lower-dimensional sequences. Finally, we demonstrate that no non-trivial binary GC sequences of degree 2 exist for lengths up to 100, and that no binary GC sequences of degree 4 exist with lengths between 1 and 1000. Furthermore, we establish that for any length $L$, a binary GC sequence of degree 2 exists if and only if $L$ is a perfect square, and a binary GC sequence of degree 4 exists if and only if $L$ is the square of a perfect square. These findings are derived from a novel construction of binary sequences with ideal autocorrelation. Additionally, we provide a new construction for PGCA sequences of degree 2 in dimension $d$ utilizing a sequence with ideal autocorrelation and a binary GC sequence of degree 2 in dimension $d-1$. Finally, we present a construction for PGCA sequences of degree 4 in dimension $d$ based on a binary GC sequence of degree 4 in dimension $d-1$. In all cases, the resulting sequences achieve the minimum possible sidelobe level. Notably, the proposed constructions for PGCA sequences of degree 2 in dimensions 2, 3, and 4 are new. This study examines the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in both molecular fluids and model potentials. We begin by analyzing the viscosity of Lennard-Jones fluids across various densities and temperatures, employing the Green-Kubo method alongside the mode-coupling theory (MCT) framework. Subsequently, we investigate molecular fluids, specifically n-butane and n-pentane, using the same computational approaches. Finally, we assess the validity of the residual entropy scaling law for viscosity, which posits that the logarithm of viscosity correlates linearly with residual entropy. Our findings indicate that this scaling holds true for Lennard-Jones fluids, n-butane, and n-pentane across a broad range of conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the residual entropy scaling law is also applicable to model potentials, including the soft-sphere and inverse-power-law systems. These results suggest that the residual entropy scaling law represents a universal phenomenon. Additionally, we explore the connection between residual entropy and the MCT exponent $\gamma$, which characterizes the divergence of viscosity near the glass transition. We show that the exponent $\gamma$ exhibits a linear dependence on residual entropy, thereby reinforcing the universality of the residual entropy scaling law. Finally, we examine the link between the MCT exponent $\gamma$ and the Adam-Gibbs parameter $z$, demonstrating that $\gamma$ scales linearly with $z$. This linear relationship between $\gamma$ and $z$ further supports the validity of the residual entropy scaling law. Overall, our findings provide strong evidence that the residual entropy scaling law is a universal phenomenon. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. The authors demonstrate that the model's predictions align with quantum mechanics only under specific constraints. Specifically, the probability distribution of hidden variables must adhere to a particular functional form, and the probability of detecting a hidden variable at a specific location must be uniform across all directions. These requirements are highly restrictive, and the authors argue that they are unlikely to be satisfied by any physically realizable model. Consequently, the paper concludes that Invariant-set theory fails to provide a viable local, deterministic, and realist explanation for the correlations found in Bell-type experiments. Furthermore, the authors contend that the theory's reliance on superdeterminism renders it unscientific, as it effectively permits any outcome to be predicted in advance. Finally, the paper addresses the criticism that the no-signaling theorem is inapplicable to superdeterministic models, arguing that this claim is unfounded. Thus, the paper maintains that Invariant-set theory is incompatible with the principles of quantum mechanics. This would essentially render the theory indistinguishable from Bohmian mechanics, which is already well-established. In such a scenario, the purported novelty of Invariant-set theory would be lost, and its scientific value would be severely diminished. The growing demand for real-time applications across diverse domains has led to the widespread adoption of Hardware Virtualization Support (HVS) in modern embedded systems. However, HVS introduces significant challenges for real-time performance, primarily due to the unpredictable execution times of virtual machine monitors (VMMs) and the overhead associated with context switches between the host and guest operating systems. This paper introduces T-Visor, a hypervisor designed to manage mixed-criticality embedded real-time systems. By integrating a real-time scheduler into the VMM, T-Visor ensures that guest operating systems meet their deadlines. Furthermore, it employs a dynamic context switching mechanism to minimize VMM execution time and reduce context switch overhead. Experimental results demonstrate that T-Visor outperforms state-of-the-art hypervisors in terms of real-time performance. Additionally, the system was evaluated using a real-time video processing application, confirming its practical applicability. The source code for T-Visor is accessible at https://github.com/visorlab/T-Visor. This study introduces a model-based probabilistic policy search (MPSP) framework designed to learn robust controllers for nonlinear systems facing both parametric and state uncertainties. The approach utilizes a nonlinear system model to forecast state trajectories under various policies, thereby identifying the most promising candidates. To address uncertainties, the method employs a Gaussian process to model the nonlinear dynamics, enabling the calculation of uncertainty bounds for predicted trajectories. Consequently, policies are optimized to minimize the probability of trajectory violations. The proposed framework is validated through numerical simulations on a nonlinear pendulum system and a nonlinear vehicle model. Simulation results demonstrate that the learned controllers effectively handle both types of uncertainties and outperform existing robust control techniques. Furthermore, the framework's applicability is confirmed by its successful deployment on a real-time robot arm. Experimental outcomes indicate that the learned controllers achieve high tracking accuracy while maintaining robustness against uncertainties. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. We investigate heritable information within stochastic dynamics, a concept where a dynamical system generates a time series of random variables that encodes a function of its initial state. This phenomenon is prevalent in natural systems, where the transmission of information from ancestors to descendants is vital for evolutionary adaptation. We establish a general framework for quantifying this heritable information and demonstrate its connection to the mutual information between random variables. Furthermore, we analyze a model of asexual evolution featuring a noisy dynamical system and a fitness function, revealing that the system's behavior converges toward a specific optimal trajectory. Finally, we explore the relationship between heritable information and the fitness landscape, showing that information increases as the landscape becomes more rugged. These findings offer a comprehensive theoretical basis for understanding heritable information in natural systems. The associated code is available at https://github.com/robertkelly1/heritable-info. This paper establishes two theorems regarding the asymptotic behavior of the $p$-th moments for hook lengths in large, random Young diagrams of shape $\lambda \vdash n$, where $p$ equals 2 or 3. Specifically, for $p=2$, the $p$-th moment is approximately $n/2$, whereas for $p=3$, it is approximately $n/3$. These findings are derived from a more comprehensive theorem that addresses the asymptotic distribution of the count of hooks in $\lambda$ divisible by a general integer $p$. Furthermore, the results for $p=2$ and $p=3$ yield new insights into the asymptotic distribution of square hook lengths and the total number of hooks in large, random Young diagrams. The proofs rely on the asymptotic Plancherel measure and the asymptotic hook length distribution within this measure, alongside an integral representation of the relevant moments. Additionally, the methodology employed generates a novel algorithm for computing the moments of the asymptotic hook length distribution. Finally, the paper concludes with a conjecture concerning the asymptotic distribution of hook lengths in large, random Young diagrams. This conjecture is substantiated by numerical evidence and a rigorous analysis of the first two moments. The authors anticipate that this conjecture will facilitate the derivation of further results, including the asymptotic distribution of the number of hooks in $\lambda$ divisible by $p$ for $p \geq 4$. The Larmor clock method measures tunneling time by analyzing the precession of a particle's spin as it traverses a potential barrier. This study employs the time of arrival operator to calculate the average spin-flip rate, thereby deriving the tunneling time. The resulting expression for tunneling time aligns with the Bohmian velocity approach and the most recent findings from the probability flux method. Furthermore, the tunneling time derived via the Larmor clock exhibits a dependence on the particle's initial spin orientation. Finally, the implications of these results for the tunneling phenomenon are discussed. We introduce a method for performing universal quantum computation using Bose-Einstein condensates. This approach relies on the nonlinear evolution of the condensate's wavefunction, which is driven by interatomic interactions. The quantum gates are implemented by applying external potentials to the system. We demonstrate that the CNOT gate can be executed with high fidelity, and we outline a strategy for achieving universal quantum computation. Additionally, we discuss the impact of thermal effects on the performance of these gates. Our findings indicate that thermal atoms can be effectively removed from the system, allowing the quantum gate to function with high precision. Furthermore, we show that the fidelity of the CNOT gate remains robust against variations in the initial state. Finally, we examine the influence of experimental imperfections on gate fidelity and conclude that the proposed scheme is feasible within current experimental capabilities. This work establishes a foundation for developing quantum technologies based on Bose-Einstein condensates. The research was conducted within the framework of the Russian Quantum Center. Intestinal parasites pose a significant global health challenge, with millions of individuals infected annually. Accurate diagnosis is essential for selecting appropriate treatments and preventing the spread of these diseases. This study introduces a deep belief network (DBN) approach to classify intestinal parasites from microscopic images. The method involves training the DBN on a dataset of 1,000 images across seven parasite categories, followed by classifying new images using the trained model. The results demonstrate that the proposed DBN-based system achieves a classification accuracy of 96.7%. This study addresses a non-zero-sum stochastic differential game concerning investment and reinsurance strategies for two competing insurance firms. The analysis incorporates both proportional and excess-of-loss reinsurance, with the underlying stock price dynamics modeled as a regime-switching jump-diffusion process. The objective is to determine the Nash equilibrium within this framework. To achieve this, we first transform the original system of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) into a linear form. Subsequently, we derive the explicit solution to this linear PDE system and identify the corresponding equilibrium strategies. Finally, we propose an efficient numerical algorithm to approximate the solution, which is validated through a numerical example. The results demonstrate that the proposed method yields accurate approximations for the Nash equilibrium, with the error remaining bounded. Furthermore, we examine the impact of various model parameters on the equilibrium strategies and the associated cost functions. These findings indicate that the proposed approach is effective and practical for solving the investment and reinsurance game. Additionally, the methodology offers a robust foundation for addressing other types of stochastic games. This work extends and generalizes several existing studies on investment and reinsurance games. Specifically, it broadens the scope of prior research by incorporating excess-of-loss reinsurance and accounting for jumps in stock price dynamics. Moreover, the paper introduces a novel approach for approximating solutions to nonlinear PDEs, a contribution that is also significant for the field of numerical analysis. The proposed algorithm is designed to be computationally efficient and well-suited for practical applications. Finally, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of the sensitivity of equilibrium strategies to different model parameters, a contribution that enhances the utility of this research for practitioners. In summary, this work represents a significant advancement in the field of stochastic games, offering valuable insights and tools for researchers and practitioners alike. We present a comprehensive analysis of low-energy pion-nucleon scattering, deriving model-independent constraints on the pion-nucleon interaction. This study utilizes a covariant dispersion relation approach, which offers a model-independent framework for analyzing scattering data and calculating amplitudes. We examine the analytic structure of these amplitudes, specifically focusing on their singularities and cuts, to establish rigorous limits on low-energy parameters. Furthermore, we incorporate recent experimental data on pion-nucleon scattering to refine our analysis. Our results indicate that the pion-nucleon interaction is predominantly of the $s$-wave type, with a small but significant $d$-wave component. Additionally, we determine the mass of the $\Delta$ resonance to be $1232 \pm 1$ MeV. These findings align with the predictions of chiral perturbation theory. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the low-energy structure of the pion-nucleon interaction. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor V. G. Barmin. This study examines the SRC distributions across various nuclei, including $^{12}$C, $^{16}$O, $^{40}$Ca, $^{48}$Ca, $^{90}$Zr, and $^{208}$Pb. The analysis utilizes the $J$-box model, which incorporates both short-range and long-range correlations alongside the Pauli exclusion principle. Results indicate that the probability of SRCs remains nearly constant across all examined nuclei, while the ratio of neutron-to-proton SRCs is approximately 0.2. Furthermore, the calculated total SRC probabilities align well with experimental data. These findings suggest that the underlying SRC mechanism remains consistent throughout the periodic table. Additionally, the study explores the potential for extending this analysis to superheavy nuclei. Finally, the research addresses the impact of SRCs on the nuclear equation of state, a critical factor in understanding neutron stars. The calculated pressure values are compared against existing experimental results. Finally, the influence of SRCs on the phase transition from quark-gluon plasma to hadronic matter is examined. The study concludes that SRCs significantly affect the equation of state, thereby altering the characteristics of the phase transition. This conclusion is supported by comparisons with other theoretical models. The findings underscore the necessity of incorporating SRCs into theoretical models to accurately describe the equation of state and the phase transition from quark-gluon plasma to hadronic matter. This work is part of a broader effort to understand the quark-gluon plasma phase and the associated phase transition. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of the current study and outlines potential directions for future research. The study also highlights the need for further experimental investigations into SRCs to validate the theoretical findings. We introduce a new dark matter detection initiative called PALEOCCENE, which utilizes a 100-gram sample of color centers embedded in a transparent, flexible polymer. This approach leverages the exceptional sensitivity of color centers to low-energy nuclear recoils, a capability demonstrated by recent experiments on both solid-state nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond and divacancies in hexagonal boron nitride. The PALEOCCENE project aims to advance this technology by employing a more abundant and robust system: nitrogen vacancies in the widely used polymer PMMA. This material offers superior optical properties, including high transparency and a narrow emission spectrum, alongside a proven history of use in quantum sensing. We outline the scientific objectives and technical specifications of the project, demonstrating that a 100-gram detector can achieve a mass sensitivity of 100 attograms per kilogram. Furthermore, we show that the experiment can reach an exposure of 100 gram-days per keV, surpassing the capabilities of current direct detection experiments. The PALEOCCENE detector is scheduled to be deployed at the SNOLAB underground facility in Sudbury, Canada, in 2024. This facility provides a low-background environment and a deep underground location, ensuring that the experiment's sensitivity exceeds that of other direct dark matter searches. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the background index, which is estimated to be below $10^{-4}$ counts/kg/day/keV. This analysis incorporates contributions from radioactive isotopes, cosmic muons, and neutrons, as well as the potential for optical background events. Finally, we demonstrate that the PALEOCCENE detector can distinguish between nuclear and electronic recoils, thereby mitigating the impact of optical backgrounds. We conclude that the PALEOCCENE detector will enable the exploration of a dark matter parameter space that is currently inaccessible to other direct detection methods. This includes sensitivity to sub-GeV dark matter with a cross section of $\sigma \sim 10^{-30}$ cm$^2$, as well as the ability to probe the nuclear recoil energy region below 100 eV, where the background index is expected to be negligible. We investigate the dynamics of active colloidal dimers within activity gradients, focusing on how these gradients influence the dimers' rotational and translational diffusion. Our findings indicate that the dimers exhibit enhanced rotational diffusion when the activity of the smaller particle exceeds that of the larger one. Conversely, the gradient can either suppress or enhance translational diffusion, contingent upon the specific dimer configuration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dimers can be trapped in regions of low activity, a phenomenon that may offer a mechanism for the self-assembly of active colloidal molecules. These conclusions are supported by both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. Finally, we outline potential experimental realizations of this system.
